title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
text:
ps.grad
Overview Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between postsecondary graduation (No = did not graduate, Y = graduated) and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. Note that individuals currently attending postsecondary are excluded from this analysis as their graduation status is not yet determined. Postsecondary graduation shows a very strong association at year 1 that weakens considerably over time, with a pattern that closely mirrors postsecondary attendance but with important distinctions in the magnitude and direction of effects.
Year 1 At one year post-graduation, postsecondary graduation shows a very strong association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer’s V=0.633). As with postsecondary attendance, this is substantially driven by the structural relationship between graduation status and the attending postsecondary outcome category — postsecondary graduates show an 83.7% rate of still attending postsecondary at year 1, reflecting those who have completed one credential and are pursuing another. Non-graduates show substantially higher rates of meaningful regional employment (19.3% vs 7.4%), not meaningful employment (31.2% vs 4.7%), and no Minnesota employment record (21.3% vs 1.7%), while graduates show markedly lower rates across all non-postsecondary outcomes at this early stage. (χ²=18207.912, df=4, Cramer’s V=0.633, p<0.001)
Year 5 By five years post-graduation the association weakens considerably but remains moderate (Cramer’s V=0.330). Non-graduates show higher rates of meaningful regional employment (25.7% vs 22.0%) and notably higher rates of no Minnesota employment record (30.7% vs 17.9%), while postsecondary graduates show higher rates of meaningful Minnesota employment (20.7% vs 15.1%) and postsecondary attendance (26.2% vs 4.5%). The divergence in no Minnesota employment record between the two groups is particularly striking — non-graduates are nearly twice as likely to have no Minnesota employment record as graduates, suggesting postsecondary graduation is strongly associated with remaining employed in Minnesota. (χ²=3791.997, df=4, Cramer’s V=0.330, p<0.001)
Year 10 At ten years post-graduation the association weakens to a weak effect (Cramer’s V=0.130). Rates of meaningful regional employment converge almost entirely between non-graduates (24.7%) and graduates (24.8%). Postsecondary graduates show a notably higher rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (27.9% vs 17.9%), while non-graduates show a higher rate of no Minnesota employment record (38.6% vs 34.3%) and not meaningful employment (18.7% vs 13.0%). The convergence in meaningful regional employment rates mirrors the pattern observed for postsecondary attendance, suggesting that by year 10 postsecondary graduation has little bearing on whether individuals are employed in the region but continues to distinguish between the quality and location of employment outcomes. (χ²=341.123, df=3, Cramer’s V=0.130, p<0.001)
Summary Postsecondary graduation shows a very strong association with workforce participation outcomes at year 1 (Cramer’s V=0.633), largely driven by structural overlap with the attending postsecondary outcome category, that weakens to a weak effect by year 10 (Cramer’s V=0.130). The most substantively important finding is the persistent and growing advantage of postsecondary graduates in achieving meaningful Minnesota employment across all time points, while non-graduates show stronger attachment to regional employment and considerably higher rates of no Minnesota employment record. By year 10 meaningful regional employment rates converge entirely between the two groups, suggesting that postsecondary graduation shapes where people work rather than whether they are meaningfully employed in the region.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
text:
ps.grad.InstitutionSector
Overview Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between the sector of postsecondary institution from which individuals graduated (1=Public 4-year, 2=Private not-for-profit 4-year, 4=Public 2-year, 11=Private other) and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. This analysis is restricted to postsecondary graduates and those currently attending, excluding individuals who never attended or did not graduate. Institution sector shows a weak but consistent association across all three time points, with substantively meaningful differences in the type of employment achieved across sectors.
Year 1 At one year post-graduation, institution sector shows a weak association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer’s V=0.149). The overwhelming majority of individuals across all sectors are still attending postsecondary at year 1, ranging from 70.5% for public 2-year graduates to 94.3% for public 4-year graduates, reflecting the expected pattern that 4-year institution graduates are more likely to be pursuing additional credentials. Among those in the workforce, public 2-year graduates show the highest rate of meaningful regional employment (15.3%), more than double the rate of public 4-year graduates (2.6%) and private not-for-profit 4-year graduates (0.9%), suggesting that 2-year institution graduates enter regional employment much more quickly. (χ²=2371.287, df=16, Cramer’s V=0.149, p<0.001)
Year 5 By five years post-graduation the association remains weak (Cramer’s V=0.161) but the patterns become considerably more interpretable as postsecondary attendance rates decline. Public 2-year graduates show by far the highest rate of meaningful regional employment (35.6%), more than double that of public 4-year graduates (16.2%) and private not-for-profit 4-year graduates (8.9%). Conversely, private not-for-profit 4-year graduates show the highest rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (28.5%), followed by public 4-year graduates (20.8%). Private other graduates show notably lower rates of no Minnesota employment record (8.3%) compared to all other sectors, while private not-for-profit 4-year graduates show the highest rate (24.2%), suggesting considerably higher out-of-state migration among graduates of private 4-year institutions. (χ²=2046.570, df=16, Cramer’s V=0.161, p<0.001)
Year 10 At ten years post-graduation the association remains weak (Cramer’s V=0.125). Public 2-year graduates continue to show the highest rate of meaningful regional employment (35.8%), more than three times that of private not-for-profit 4-year graduates (11.2%) and substantially higher than public 4-year graduates (21.0%) and private other graduates (24.6%). Public 4-year and private not-for-profit 4-year graduates show similar rates of meaningful Minnesota employment (30.7% and 33.7% respectively), while public 2-year graduates show the lowest rate (20.8%). Private not-for-profit 4-year graduates show the highest rate of no Minnesota employment record (40.3%), while public 2-year graduates show the lowest (28.7%). (χ²=519.468, df=9, Cramer’s V=0.125, p<0.001)
Summary Postsecondary graduation institution sector shows a weak but consistent association with workforce participation outcomes across all three time points (Cramer’s V=0.149, 0.161, 0.125). Despite the modest effect sizes, the findings are substantively compelling and tell a clear story — public 2-year institution graduates show the strongest and most persistent attachment to regional employment across all time points, with meaningful regional employment rates remaining above 35% at both years 5 and 10. In contrast, private not-for-profit 4-year graduates show the strongest tendency toward meaningful Minnesota employment and the highest rates of no Minnesota employment record, suggesting these graduates are the most geographically mobile and least likely to remain in the region. Public 4-year graduates occupy a middle position, showing moderate rates of both regional and Minnesota employment. These findings have direct implications for regional workforce development, suggesting that 2-year institution pathways are particularly important for regional talent retention.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
text:
highest.cred.level
Overview Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between highest credential level attained (No college, Some college, Less than Associate Degree, Associate Degree, Attending ps, Bachelor Degree, Master Degree or higher) and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. Highest credential level shows a strong association at year 1 that weakens considerably over time, with substantively meaningful patterns in how credential level shapes the type and location of employment achieved.
Year 1 At one year post-graduation, highest credential level shows a strong association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer’s V=0.378). At this early stage the results are heavily influenced by the structural relationship between credential level and the attending postsecondary outcome category, with postsecondary attendance rates increasing monotonically with credential level — from 0% for no college to 93.0% for master degree or higher. Among those in the workforce, a clear gradient emerges in meaningful regional employment, declining with higher credential levels — from 21.7% for no college to 1.9% for master degree or higher. Conversely, no college individuals show the highest rates of not meaningful employment (39.7%) and no Minnesota employment record (31.6%). (χ²=27300.114, df=24, Cramer’s V=0.378, p<0.001)
Year 5 By five years post-graduation the association weakens to a moderate effect (Cramer’s V=0.246) as credential attainment becomes more fully realized. A notable and substantively important pattern emerges — individuals with less than associate degree (35.1%) and associate degree (32.1%) show the highest rates of meaningful regional employment, considerably higher than bachelor degree (16.5%) and master degree or higher (8.1%) holders. The inverse is true for meaningful Minnesota employment, where bachelor degree (23.5%) and master degree or higher (11.8%) holders show lower regional but higher out-of-region employment rates. Master degree or higher individuals show the highest rate of still attending postsecondary (72.9%), reflecting ongoing graduate education. No college individuals show the highest rate of no Minnesota employment record (36.3%). (χ²=8561.286, df=24, Cramer’s V=0.246, p<0.001)
Year 10 At ten years post-graduation the association weakens to a weak effect (Cramer’s V=0.111). The patterns observed at year 5 persist and clarify further. Less than associate degree (34.4%) and associate degree (33.1%) holders continue to show the highest rates of meaningful regional employment, while bachelor degree (31.3%) and master degree or higher (29.1%) holders show the highest rates of meaningful Minnesota employment. Master degree or higher holders show the highest rate of no Minnesota employment record (43.3%), suggesting the highest credential level is associated with the greatest geographic mobility and lowest regional retention. No college and some college individuals show relatively similar distributions across outcome categories, suggesting that without any credential attainment the long-term workforce trajectory is similar regardless of whether some postsecondary was attempted. (χ²=746.232, df=15, Cramer’s V=0.111, p<0.001)
Summary Highest credential level shows a strong association with workforce participation outcomes at year 1 (Cramer’s V=0.378) that weakens to a weak effect by year 10 (Cramer’s V=0.111). The most substantively important finding is the clear and persistent inverse relationship between credential level and regional workforce attachment — sub-baccalaureate credential holders (less than associate and associate degree) show the strongest regional employment rates across all time points, while bachelor and master degree holders show increasing tendencies toward meaningful Minnesota employment and out-of-state migration. This pattern is consistent with and reinforces findings from the institution sector analysis, where public 2-year graduates showed the strongest regional attachment, and aligns with the broader pattern observed across academic achievement variables suggesting that higher educational attainment is associated with employment outside the region in Southwest Minnesota.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
text:
ps.grad.location
Overview Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between the location of postsecondary graduation (Did not graduate ps, PS grad MN, PS grad outside MN, PS grad region) and workforce participation outcomes at 1, 5, and 10 years after high school graduation. This variable is uniquely relevant to the regional workforce development focus of this study, as it directly captures whether individuals pursued and completed postsecondary education within the Southwest Minnesota region, elsewhere in Minnesota, or outside the state. The association is weak but consistent across all three time points, with substantively compelling patterns in regional workforce attachment by graduation location.
Year 1 At one year post-graduation, graduation location shows a weak association with workforce participation outcomes (Cramer’s V=0.158). Among those in the workforce rather than attending postsecondary, regional graduates show the strongest attachment to meaningful regional employment (56.2%), substantially higher than PS grad MN (35.5%), PS grad outside MN (38.2%), and did not graduate ps (24.6%). Did not graduate ps individuals show the highest rates of not meaningful employment (40.0%) and no Minnesota employment record (27.3%), while regional graduates show the lowest rate of no Minnesota employment record (6.2%), suggesting that graduating from a regional institution is strongly associated with immediate regional workforce engagement. (χ²=1514.441, df=9, Cramer’s V=0.158, p<0.001)
Year 5 By five years post-graduation the association strengthens modestly (Cramer’s V=0.191). Regional graduates continue to show the highest rate of meaningful regional employment (42.4%), considerably higher than PS grad MN (23.9%), PS grad outside MN (23.9%), and did not graduate ps (26.9%). PS grad MN graduates show the highest rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (40.9%), while PS grad outside MN graduates show a strikingly high rate of no Minnesota employment record (47.4%), suggesting that graduating outside Minnesota is strongly associated with long-term out-of-state retention. Regional graduates show the lowest rate of no Minnesota employment record (13.4%), reinforcing the strong regional retention associated with regional graduation. (χ²=3181.250, df=9, Cramer’s V=0.191, p<0.001)
Year 10 At ten years post-graduation the association remains weak (Cramer’s V=0.162). Regional graduates continue to show the highest rate of meaningful regional employment (36.9%), significantly higher than PS grad MN (20.4%), PS grad outside MN (18.0%), and did not graduate ps (24.8%). PS grad MN graduates show the highest rate of meaningful Minnesota employment (38.0%), while PS grad outside MN graduates maintain the highest rate of no Minnesota employment record (54.8%) — the highest rate of out-of-state retention observed for any subgroup across all variables examined. Regional graduates show the lowest rate of no Minnesota employment record (23.2%), the lowest of any graduation location group across all time points. (χ²=1582.788, df=9, Cramer’s V=0.162, p<0.001)
Summary Postsecondary graduation location shows a weak but consistent and substantively compelling association with workforce participation outcomes across all three time points (Cramer’s V=0.158, 0.191, 0.162). Despite the modest effect sizes, the findings tell a clear and policy-relevant story. Regional graduates show the strongest and most persistent attachment to meaningful regional employment at every time point, with rates consistently 10-15 percentage points higher than other graduation location groups by years 5 and 10. Conversely, graduating outside Minnesota is associated with the highest rates of no Minnesota employment record at all time points, reaching 54.8% by year 10. PS grad MN graduates occupy a middle position, showing strong meaningful Minnesota employment but moderate regional attachment. These findings strongly suggest that the location of postsecondary graduation is one of the most direct predictors of long-term regional workforce retention, with regional institutions playing a critical role in keeping graduates employed in Southwest Minnesota.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
section: Categorical Variables - Ranked by Cramer’s V at Year 1
text:
Categorical Variables - Ranked by Cramer’s V at Year 1

PS Attendance (Cramer’s V: 0.698, 0.295, 0.108) The strongest association at year 1 but substantially inflated by structural overlap with the attending postsecondary outcome category. Association weakens considerably over time. Long-term finding: non-attendees show stronger regional attachment while attendees gravitate toward meaningful Minnesota employment.
PS Graduation (Cramer’s V: 0.633, 0.330, 0.130) Similarly inflated at year 1 by structural overlap. Weakens considerably over time. Long-term finding: graduates show higher rates of meaningful Minnesota employment while non-graduates show stronger regional attachment and higher rates of no Minnesota employment record.
ACT Participation (Cramer’s V: 0.430, 0.225, 0.137) The strongest non-structurally-inflated predictor and the most meaningful high school accomplishment variable. Non-ACT students show strong and persistent regional workforce attachment across all time points, while ACT takers are strongly associated with postsecondary attendance and subsequent out-of-region employment.
Highest Credential Level (Cramer’s V: 0.378, 0.246, 0.111) A strong association at year 1 that weakens over time. A clear inverse relationship emerges between credential level and regional attachment — sub-baccalaureate credential holders show the strongest regional employment rates while bachelor and master degree holders increasingly gravitate toward out-of-region employment and out-of-state migration.
PSEO Participation (Cramer’s V: 0.370, 0.165, 0.087) Strong at year 1, largely reflecting direct relationship with postsecondary attendance. PSEO participants show persistent tendency toward meaningful Minnesota employment over regional employment, suggesting broader geographic mobility associated with early college experience.
Economic Status (Cramer’s V: 0.285, 0.127, 0.094) The strongest demographic predictor, particularly at year 1. Economically disadvantaged students enter the workforce earlier but into less stable employment, while non- disadvantaged students pursue postsecondary at higher rates. Differences narrow considerably by years 5 and 10.
Special Education Status (Cramer’s V: 0.265, 0.149, 0.097) A moderate association at year 1 that weakens over time. Special education students enter the workforce earlier and show a persistent tendency toward regional over Minnesota employment across all time points.
AP Exam Participation (Cramer’s V: 0.217, 0.146, 0.089) Moderate at year 1, weakening over time. Mirrors the ACT participation pattern — AP exam takers show persistent tendency toward out-of-region employment while non-takers show stronger regional attachment.
English Learner Status (Cramer’s V: 0.214, 0.086, 0.059) Moderate at year 1, weakening considerably over time. English learners enter the workforce earlier but into less stable situations, with persistent challenges in achieving meaningful Minnesota employment through year 10.
Non-English Home Language (Cramer’s V: 0.178, 0.058, 0.047) Closely mirrors English learner status throughout, consistent with the strong overlap between these variables identified during MCA. Slightly weaker associations at all time points.
PS Grad Location (Cramer’s V: 0.158, 0.191, 0.162) A weak but remarkably stable association that is among the most substantively important findings of the entire analysis. Regional graduates show the strongest and most persistent regional employment attachment at every time point, while graduating outside Minnesota is associated with the highest rates of no Minnesota employment record, reaching 54.8% by year 10.
PS Grad Institution Sector (Cramer’s V: 0.149, 0.161, 0.125) Weak but stable across all time points. Public 2-year institution graduates show the strongest regional attachment while private not-for-profit 4-year graduates show the highest geographic mobility. Directly reinforces the graduation location findings.
Race/Ethnicity (Cramer’s V: 0.108, 0.044, 0.047) Weak and declining association. Notable patterns include persistent workforce challenges for AI students and higher rates of no Minnesota employment record among all minority groups at year 10. Small sample sizes for minority groups warrant cautious interpretation.
Gender (Cramer’s V: 0.097, 0.093, 0.056) Consistently weak across all time points. Females more likely to pursue postsecondary immediately after graduation while males transition more quickly into regional employment, though differences narrow considerably by year 10.
EDR (Cramer’s V: 0.079, 0.110, 0.124) Weak but uniquely strengthening over time. EDR 6E Southwest Central students show a growing advantage in meaningful Minnesota employment while EDR 8 Southwest students show increasing rates of no Minnesota employment record, suggesting growing geographic divergence within the region.
CTE Achievement (Cramer’s V: 0.075, 0.090, 0.088) The weakest categorical predictor but with a substantively important and stable pattern. CTE Concentrators or Completors show the highest rates of meaningful regional employment at every time point, with No CTE students showing strikingly high rates of no Minnesota employment record by year 10 (43.8%).
Community Demographic Description (Cramer’s V: 0.057, 0.072, 0.079) The weakest categorical predictor overall but also strengthening over time. Urban/town/rural mix students increasingly gravitate toward out-of-region employment while town/rural mix and entirely rural students show stronger regional attachment.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
section: Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared at Year 1
text:
Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared at Year 1

MCA Math (η²: 0.168, 0.025, 0.017) The strongest continuous predictor at year 1 with a large effect size, the largest observed for any continuous variable. A distinctive early pattern shows lower Math scores associated with both not meaningful employment and no Minnesota employment record — unique among MCA subjects. By year 10 the meaningful regional employment group shows the lowest Math scores of all groups.
MCA Reading (η²: 0.129, 0.023, 0.057) The second strongest continuous predictor at year 1 with a large effect size, notable for its unique trajectory — weakening to a small effect at year 5 before strengthening to a medium effect at year 10. The only continuous variable to strengthen at year 10, suggesting Reading achievement becomes increasingly predictive of out-of-region employment over time.
ACT Composite Score (η²: 0.093, 0.038, 0.028) A moderate effect at year 1 weakening to small over time. The attending postsecondary group shows substantially higher scores than all workforce-engaged groups, and the meaningful regional employment group shows progressively lower scores relative to other groups over time.
MCA Science (η²: 0.085, 0.033, 0.019) A large effect at year 1 weakening to small over time. Results should be interpreted with caution given the voluntary and self-selected nature of Science MCA participation. Pattern mirrors Reading and Math, with regional employment consistently showing the lowest Science scores.
Total CTE Courses Taken (η²: 0.032, 0.027, 0.028) A small but remarkably stable effect across all three time points, unique among continuous variables. The meaningful regional employment group shows the highest number of CTE courses taken at every time point, with the gap between regional and out-of-region employment groups growing over time.
Average Wages as Percentage of State Average (η²: 0.010, 0.004, 0.006) A negligible effect throughout, explaining at most 1% of variance. Despite very small effect sizes, regional employment consistently shows higher relative wages than meaningful Minnesota employment, suggesting competitive regional wages relative to the broader state labor market.
Average Unemployment Rate (η²: 0.005, 0.015, 0.032) The weakest predictor at year 1 but growing to a small effect by year 10. Individuals with no Minnesota employment record consistently experience lower unemployment rates, likely reflecting out-of-state migration to stronger labor markets.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
section: Key Themes Across All Variable Groups
text:
Key Themes Across All Variable Groups
Three overarching themes emerge from the analysis:
The first is a persistent academic achievement gradient in geographic mobility. Across virtually every academic achievement variable — ACT participation, AP exam, PSEO, MCA scores, ACT composite, and credential level — higher achievement is consistently associated with postsecondary attendance and subsequent employment outside the region. This pattern strengthens over time and is one of the most robust findings of the entire analysis.
The second is the importance of CTE and vocational pathways for regional retention. In direct contrast to the academic achievement pattern, CTE engagement variables — CTE achievement, total CTE courses taken, and by extension public 2-year institution graduation and sub-baccalaureate credentials — are consistently associated with stronger regional workforce attachment across all time points. This divergence between academic and CTE pathways has direct implications for regional workforce development policy.
The third is the critical role of postsecondary geography. Where individuals attend and graduate from postsecondary education is among the most stable and policy-relevant predictors of long-term regional workforce retention. Regional postsecondary graduation is associated with the strongest regional employment attachment while out-of-state graduation is associated with the highest rates of permanent out-of-state migration. This finding points directly to the strategic importance of regional postsecondary institutions for Southwest Minnesota workforce development.

The dataset has 3,302,237 rows and 6 columns. Here are the columns and their definitions.

EnrollmentBeginTimeID: Begin date for the student’s period of attendance.
EnrollmentEndTimeID: End date for the student’s period of attendance.
OPEID: Office of Postsecondary Education (OPE)/FICE code of the college that the student attended (Foreign Key to IPEDSCharacteristics).
InstitutionName: Name of institution
EnrollmentStatus: The last enrollment status reported for the student. This field will have ‘N/A’ or “NULL” if the reporting college has not defined the student’s enrollment status as directory information. Here are the code definitions;

F: Full-time
Q: Three-quarter time
H: Half-time
L: Less than half-time
A: Leave of absence
W: Withdrawn
D: Deceased


Essentially, this dataset provides semester-based information - each observation is a semester/single period with the institutional information and beginning and end time of that single period (usually a semester). For example, if an individual attended South Dakota State University, attended in a “typical” fashion (fall and spring semesters), and graduated in 4 years, there would be 8 observations for that PersonID - one observation per semester.
There are a few pieces of information that I want to consolidate from this dataset;

Did the PersonID in the master dataset attend a college - yes or no?
Did the PersonID attend college during high school (PSEO), immediately after graduation or wait?
Did the PersonID attend multiple colleges - yes or no?
What type of college did the PersonID attend first?
Did the PersonID attend a public, private not-for-profit, or private or, for-profit college(s)?
At any point during their college career, did the PersonID attend a college(s) inside or outside of the Southwest Region or outside the County of their high school?

I was going to include the length of time that a PersonID attended college, but due to differences in how institutions report enrollment periods, it didn’t seem like it would be a great indicator.
The pieces of information missing in the original dataset is location and type of institution attended.To do this we will need to join the original dataset with an IPEDS dataset using opeid.
The IPEDS data and the NSC data will only match using the first 6 digits of the IPEDS OPEID values. So I will change that in the NSC data. Then I can join.

  select(Unitid, OPEID.6, City, State, FIPS, GeographicRegion, CountyCode, InstitutionSector, InstitutionName)  %>%

As expected, we have the same number of rows as the original master dataset - 54,063 rows. Here are the explanations of all the new columns added to the master dataset.

attended.ps - this is a confirmation that the PersonID attended a post-secondary institution at some point after graduating high school.
attended.ps.years.hsgrad - the number of years after graduation that a PersonID attended a post-secondary education. In some cases, the value is negative indicating that the PersonID attended a post-secondary institution before graduating high school.
attended.ps.within.first.year.hsgrad - did the PersonID attend a post-secondary education institution within 1 year or less from graduating high school.
n.institutions - how many post-secondary institutions the PersonID attended
first.InstitutionSector - the sector of the first post-secondary institution attended.
InstitutionSector - The sector of the post-secondary institution attended (could be multiple)
ps.in.same.ruca - did the PersonID attend a post-secondary institution in the same RUCA category as their high school
ps.in.same.edr - did the PersonID attend a post-secondary institution in the same economic development region as high school
ps.in.same.pr - did the PersonID attend a post-secondary institution in the same planning region as high school
ps.in.MN = did the PersonID attend a post-secondary institution in Minnesota.

The AP dataset has 299,631 observations and 5 columns. Each observation represents an AP exam taken so this means that a PersonID can be listed multiple times if the individual took multiple AP exams. The ExamGrade is on a 1 - 5 scale with the highest scores being better. According to Meredith at OHE, colleges give credit if the score is 3 or higher.
I’m a bit torn here. There seems to be three approaches to how I can utilize this data in the model.

I could either just create a category of whether an individual took an AP exam and not care what the grade was.
I could only use individuals who scored 3 or higher.
I could keep all the data and change it so that each observation represents a PersonID and new columns created for each AP exam and their score.

For now, I think I’m going to just utilize option 1 - whether they took an AP exam or not.

title: Employment
text:
Filter for “meaningful” employment
The biggest issue is how do we get a meaningful indicator on whether they were employed in the region and whether they are employed in an industry that matches their CTE experience that wasn’t just a “summer job”. We need to filter out summer jobs between college years, as well as adapt to different paths that students take.
We will define “meaningful employment” as an employment experience in which an individual works for one particular employer for 1,000 hours worked in any given year.
However, this isn’t going to just be checking to see if an individual has worked at an employer for 1,000 hours at graduation year, grad year +2, grad year +7 and grad year +12. Rather, it’s going to be checking on whether they are working at an employer at grad year, grad year +2, grad year +7 and grad year +12 for which they worked 1,000 hours for an given year.
For example, a person may be employed with an employer for a few years working full-time, but part-way through grad year +7, they decide to move on. I want to make sure we capture that that individual was employed in meaningful employment even though it wasn’t full-time that particular year.
The same can go the other way. Perhaps an individual just starts employment at grad year +7 but does work full-time with that particular employer form multiple years. We will want to count that as well.
In addition, I want to capture if someone is working at an employer but isn’t quite “meaningful” but turns into meaningful later on. We will count that as well.
This will be a couple step process.

First, we will filter out the employment.original data so that only meaningful employment for each PersonID is included along with the years worked at EmploymentOrganizationID.
Collect EmploymentOrganizationID for all the years that each PersonID worked meaningful employment.
Create a new datalist of each PersonID in the master datalist with grad year, grad year +2, and +7.
Then, we will cross reference the grad year list with employment year to see if meaningful employment matches.

We will end with the following columns and labels;

PersonID has had meaningful employment since graduating high school (Grad year, grad year +2, grad year +7)

No MN emp record - Has no MN emp record
No meaningful emp - Has MN emp record but never
Meaningful emp - Has MN emp record and is meaningful
After 2023 - the grad year +X is after 2023.




meaningful.employer <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, CalendarYear) %>%
  summarize(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked = sum(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  filter(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked > 999) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  distinct(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID) %>%
  right_join(mn.emp.record[,c(1)], by = "PersonID")

Now we want to merge this with all the PersonID from the master dataset so we end up with a list that has each PersonID, a column that represents grad year, and grad year +2 and +7, and confirmation on whether they had meaningful employment during those years.

master.personid.meaningful.emp <- meaningful.emp.grad.years %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.years, meaningful.emp) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, grad.years) %>%
  mutate(meaningful.emp = "Meaningful emp") %>%
  right_join(grad.years[,c(1)], by = "PersonID") %>%
  complete(PersonID, grad.years, fill = list(meaningful.emp = "No meaningful emp")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(grad.years)) %>%
  mutate(label = paste("meaningful.emp.", grad.years, sep = "")) %>%
  select(PersonID, label, meaningful.emp) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = label, values_from = meaningful.emp) %>%
  left_join(mn.emp.record, by = "PersonID") %>%
  select(PersonID, 5,6,7,2,3,4) %>%

title: Employment

Match meaningful employment and high school locations/regions.
Now, we want to determine if the locations of meaningful employment match the counties and regions from which they graduated high school. To do this, we will import the latest master dataset so we can compare their high school locations with meaningful employment locations.
Here are the columns and labels that I need;

PersonID has had meaningful employment within the county/region (Grad year, grad year +2, grad year +7)

No MN emp record - has no MN employment record
No meaningful emp - Has MN emp record but not meaningful
No location match - Has MN emp record, had meaningful employment, but no match with region
Location match - Has MN emp record, had meaningful employment, and had meaningful employment in county/region
After 2023 - the grad year +X is after 2023




emp.original.locations <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4)),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Shakopee Mdewakanton Community", "Scott"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen")) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions.1, by = c("CountyName" = "Name")) %>%
  select(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, EconomicDevelopmentRegionName, CountyName, project.pr) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, EconomicDevelopmentRegionName, CountyName, project.pr) %>%
  rename(employment.county = CountyName,
         emp.edr = EconomicDevelopmentRegionName,
         emp.pr = project.pr) %>%
  mutate(emp.edr = str_replace(emp.edr, "  ", " "),
         emp.edr = as.factor(emp.edr),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, " County", ""),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen"),
         employment.county = as.factor(employment.county)) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions[,c(2,4)], by = c("employment.county" = "Name")) %>%
  rename(emp.Dem_Desc = Dem_Desc) 

meaningful.emp.locations <- meaningful.emp.grad.years %>%
  left_join(emp.original.locations, by = c("PersonID", "year" = "CalendarYear", "EmploymentOrganizationID")) %>%
  mutate(emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)", "Unknown", as.character(emp.edr)),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)", "Unknown", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Hennepin", "EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Ramsey", "EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "St. Louis", "EDR 3 - Arrowhead", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Unknown", "Unknown", emp.edr),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "Unknown", "Unknown", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "NULL", "NULL", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Mahnomen", "EDR 2 - Headwaters", emp.edr))

grad.locations <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-10.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID, county.name, Dem_Desc, edr, planning.region) %>%

         hs.Dem_Desc = Dem_Desc,

grad.emp.location.match <- grad.locations %>%
  right_join(meaningful.emp.locations, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(county.match = ifelse(employment.county == hs.county.name, 1,
                               ifelse(employment.county %in%  c("Unknown", "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)"), 0, -1)),
         edr.match = ifelse(emp.edr == hs.edr, 1,
                            ifelse(emp.edr == "Unknown", 0, -1)),
         region.match = ifelse(emp.pr %in% c("Southwest"), 1,
                               ifelse(emp.edr == "Unknown", 0, -1)),

  group_by(PersonID, grad.years) %>%
  summarize(county.match = max(county.match),
         edr.match = max(edr.match),

  ungroup() %>%

title: Employment
section: Match employment industry with career cluster
text:
Match employment industry with career cluster
Next we need to find a way to compare the CTE careerclusters with the actual industry from which they work. We are not able to compare majors which is a bummer. But, the careerclusters from CTE coursework does align somewhat with NAICS codes. Here’s what it looks like;

careercluster.naics.cw <- read_xlsx('/Users/kellyasche/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY27/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/Employment/career-cluster-naics.xlsx') %>%
  rename(cw.CareerCluster = `Career cluster code`,
         cw.CareerClusterName = `Career Cluster`,
         cw.emp.ind.code = 3,
         cw.emp.ind.name = 4)


datatable(careercluster.naics.cw, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(columnDefs = list(list(className = "dt-center", targets = 1:3)))) 






There is one industry in which two career clusters will have to be marged - Human Services and Health Science & Health Occupations. Due to this, we will create a new column with an “updated” careercluster code that includes the merged cluster.
Here are the columns and labels that I will use;

PersonID has had meaningful employment in industry from a CTE course taken (Grad year, grad year +2, grad year +7)

No MN emp record - has no MN employment record
No meaningful emp - Has MN emp record nut not meaningful
No ind match - Has MN emp record, was meaningful, but industry does not match CTE course taken
Ind match - Has MN emp record, was meaningful, and industry and cTE course match.
After 2023 - the grad year +X is after 2023


Step 1 is to determine the industry codes for each PersonID that experienced meaningful employment for each of their “grad years”.


emp.original.for.cw <- employment.original %>%

cc.cw.meaningful.emp <- meaningful.emp.grad.years %>%

         ind.code = as.integer(ind.code)) %>%
  left_join(careercluster.naics.cw, by = c("ind.code" = "cw.emp.ind.code"))

grad.cc <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-10.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID, 22:46) %>%
  gather(key = "cte", value = "n.courses", 2:ncol(.)) %>%

  left_join(grad.cc, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(cc.ind.match = ifelse(is.na(n.courses), -1,
                               ifelse(cw.CareerCluster == cte.cw, 1, 0)),
         cc.ind.match = ifelse(ind.code == 54, 1, cc.ind.match)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, grad.years) %>%
  summarize(max.match = max(cc.ind.match)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(cc.ind.match = ifelse(max.match == -1, "No CTE",
                               ifelse(max.match == 0, "No ind match", "Ind match")),
         cc.ind.match = ifelse(is.na(cc.ind.match), "No crosswalk", cc.ind.match)) %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.years, cc.ind.match) %>%
  complete(PersonID, grad.years) %>%
  mutate(label = paste("ind.match.", grad.years, sep = "")) %>%
  select(PersonID, label, cc.ind.match) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = label, values_from = cc.ind.match)

master.personid.grad.cc.cw.naics <- master.personid.grad.emp.location.match %>%

title: Employment
section: High school grad and employment instance match
text:
High school grad and employment instance match
First, let’s look what percentage of individuals had an employment instance where the employer was located in the same county as their high school.


match.region.summary.total.county <- master.11 %>%
  select(PersonID, hs.grad.year.county.match, hs.grad.year.2.county.match, hs.grad.year.7.county.match) %>%
  gather(key = "hs.grad.year", value = "county.match", 2:4) %>%
  filter(county.match != "After 2023") %>%
  group_by(hs.grad.year, county.match) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(hs.grad.year) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(data_id = seq(n()),
         hs.grad.year = str_sub(hs.grad.year, 1, 14),
         hs.grad.year = str_replace(hs.grad.year, "hs.grad.year.c", "hs.grad.year"))

match.region.summary.total.county.plot <- ggplot(match.region.summary.total.county, aes(hs.grad.year, pct, fill = county.match, group = county.match)) +
  geom_col_interactive(position = "dodge", aes(data_id = data_id, tooltip = paste(hs.grad.year, "\nEmployment match high school county? - ", county.match, sep = ""))) +
  geom_label(aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = .1)), show.legend = FALSE, color = "white", size = 5, position = position_dodge(width = .9)) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x="", y = "", color="", title = "Percent of individuals with meaningful employment in high school\ncounty")+
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent)+
  theme_bar+
  scale_fill_manual(values = brewer.pal(n = 6, "RdYlBu"),
                    guide = guide_legend(ncol = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        text = element_text(size = 18))

In the original dataset we have 1832415 rows and 18 columns. Below is a description of each variable.

Empl_TimeID: Last day of fiscal quarter
CalendarYear: Year
CalendarQuarter: Quarter within the year in which the data applies. Quarters are;

1 = Jan - Mar
2 = Apr - Jun
3 = Jul - Sep
4 = Oct - Dec

EmploymentOrganizationID: An internal identification for each employer.
EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked: The total number of hours worked by an employee at an employer’s location during a specific calendar quarter
EmployeeQuarterlyWages: The total wages earned by an employee at an employer’s location during a specific calendar quarter
EmployeeTenure: The total number of quarters a worker has been employeed by an organization at a specific location, up to an including the current calendar quarter
IndustryID: Auto generated ID code for a record in the Industry dimension.
USIndustryCode: Six-digit North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) code
GroupCode: Four-digit North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) code
IndustryGroup: Definition of GroupCode variable, the 4-digit NAICS code
OwnershipCode: A classification system based upon the controlling interest of the establishment primarily designed to distinguish between governmental and non-governmental establishments

10 = Federal government
20 = State government
30 = Local government
50 = Private

EmployerLocationTotalWagesPaid: The total wages paid to all workers employeed by an organization at a specific location during a specific calendar quarter
QuarterlyAverageEmployment: The average number of workers employeed by an organization at a specific location during a specific calendar quarter
LocationID: ???
EconomicDevelopmentRegion: The 13 economic development regions within the state of Minnesota as defined by the Department of Employment and Economic Development (DEED).

R01000 EDR 1 - Northwest

R02000 EDR 2 - Headwaters

R03000 EDR 3 - Arrowhead

R04000 EDR 4 - West Central

R05000 EDR 5 - North Central

R06E00 EDR 6E - Southwest Central

R06W00 EDR 6W - Upper Minnesota Valley

R07E00 EDR 7E - East Central

R07W00 EDR 7W - Central

R08000 EDR 8 - Southwest

R09000 EDR 9 - South Central

R10000 EDR 10 - Southeast
R11000 EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities

EconomicDevelopmentRegionName: Name of EDR
County: Minnesota county code to which this institution belongs. This can be used as a foreign key into the Geography dimension on MNCounty.

Link to codes

CountyName: The name of the county corresponding to the County and MNCounty Codes for this Location.
MNCounty: County Code for this location as assigned by the state of Minnesota.

Link to codes City: All of the city data is NA



So all the previous datasets we structured and filtered so that each observation in the master dataset was an individual. We will want to continue to do the same. So we need to create an employment dataset with the following columns;

PersonID
High school graduation year
Whether the individual had an employment record the year of, and each subsequent year, of high school graduation.
How many years after graduation each employment check is (i.e. grad.year.1, grad.year.2,….etc.)





grad.years <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-10.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID, hs.grad.year) %>%
  filter(hs.grad.year < 2024)

mn.emp.record.year <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  select(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  mutate(mn.emp.record = "MN emp record") %>%
  filter(CalendarYear > 2007, 
         CalendarYear < 2024) %>%
  complete(PersonID, CalendarYear, fill = list(mn.emp.record = "No MN emp record")) 

mn.emp.record <- grad.years %>%
  left_join(mn.emp.record.year, by = c("PersonID")) %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = ifelse(is.na(CalendarYear), hs.grad.year, CalendarYear),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(is.na(mn.emp.record), "No MN emp record", mn.emp.record),
         update = ifelse(CalendarYear < hs.grad.year, "Not graduated HS", "Graduated")) %>%
  filter(update == "Graduated") %>%
  select(-update) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(grad.year.seq = seq(n())) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  complete(PersonID, grad.year.seq) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  fill(hs.grad.year, .direction = "down") %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = ifelse(is.na(CalendarYear), hs.grad.year + (grad.year.seq - 1), CalendarYear),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", mn.emp.record),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(is.na(mn.emp.record), "No MN emp record", mn.emp.record),
         grad.year = paste("grad.year.", grad.year.seq-1, sep = "")) %>%
  select(-grad.year.seq)

The dataset above provides each unique PersonID from our master list along with each possible grad year and subsequent years (grad.year.0, grad.year.1, grad.year.2 … grad.year.11).
Here is the logic;

grad.year.x > 2023: mn.emp.record == “After 2023”,
if there’s a MN employment record for the PersonID and the grad.year.x: mn.emp.record == “MN emp record”
if there’s no MN employment record for the PersonID and the grad.year.x: mn.emp.record == “No MN emp record”

There are 813,280 rows in this dataset with 50,830 individuals.




The biggest issue is how do we get a meaningful indicator on whether they were employed in the region and whether they are employed in an industry that matches their CTE experience that wasn’t just a “summer job”. We need to filter out summer jobs between college years, as well as adapt to different paths that students take.
We will define “meaningful employment” as an employment experience in which an individual works for one particular employer for 1,000 hours worked in any given year.
This will be a couple step process. First we will build a dataset that has each grad.year.x from each PersonID high school graduation year and match it with the MN employment records. We will end up with each PersonID having each grad.year.x along with wither they have a MN employment record, whether they had meaningful employment, whether grad.year.x is after 2019, or whether they have no MN employment record.


meaningful.employer <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, CalendarYear) %>%
  summarize(AnnualHoursWorked = sum(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  right_join(mn.emp.record, by = c("PersonID", "CalendarYear")) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = fct_relevel(grad.year, "grad.year.0", "grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5", "grad.year.6", "grad.year.7", "grad.year.8", "grad.year.9", "grad.year.10", "grad.year.11"),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(AnnualHoursWorked > 999, "Meaningful employment", mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", new.mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(new.mn.emp.record == "MN emp record", "MN emp record - not meaningful", new.mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(mn.emp.record == "No MN emp record", "No MN emp record", new.mn.emp.record),
         meaningful.emp.code = ifelse(new.mn.emp.record == "Meaningful employment", 1, 0)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  filter(meaningful.emp.code == max(meaningful.emp.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  distinct(PersonID, grad.year, meaningful.emp.code, .keep_all = TRUE)

Now, we want to determine if the locations of meaningful employment match the counties and regions from which they graduated high school. To do this, we will import the latest master dataset so we can compare their high school locations with meaningful employment locations.

  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4)),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),

meaningful.emp.locations <- meaningful.employer %>%
  left_join(emp.original.locations, by = c("PersonID", "CalendarYear", "EmploymentOrganizationID")) %>%

         update = ifelse(CalendarYear < hs.grad.year, "Not graduated HS", "Graduated")) %>%
  filter(update == "Graduated") %>%
  select(-update) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(grad.year.seq = seq(n())) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  complete(PersonID, grad.year.seq) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  fill(hs.grad.year, .direction = "down") %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = ifelse(is.na(CalendarYear), hs.grad.year + (grad.year.seq - 1), CalendarYear),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", mn.emp.record),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(is.na(mn.emp.record), "No MN emp record", mn.emp.record),
         grad.year = paste("grad.year.", grad.year.seq-1, sep = "")) %>%
  select(-grad.year.seq)

Here is the logic;

title: Employment states each year
text:
The biggest issue is how do we get a meaningful indicator on whether they were employed in the region and whether they are employed in an industry that matches their CTE experience that wasn’t just a “summer job”. We need to filter out summer jobs between college years, as well as adapt to different paths that students take.
We will define “meaningful employment” as an employment experience in which an individual works for one particular employer for 1,000 hours worked in any given year.
This will be a couple step process. First we will build a dataset that has each grad.year.x from each PersonID high school graduation year and match it with the MN employment records. We will end up with each PersonID having each grad.year.x along with wither they have a MN employment record, whether they had meaningful employment, whether grad.year.x is after 2019, or whether they have no MN employment record.


meaningful.employer <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, CalendarYear) %>%
  summarize(AnnualHoursWorked = sum(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  right_join(mn.emp.record, by = c("PersonID", "CalendarYear")) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = fct_relevel(grad.year, "grad.year.0", "grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5", "grad.year.6", "grad.year.7", "grad.year.8", "grad.year.9", "grad.year.10", "grad.year.11"),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(AnnualHoursWorked > 999, "Meaningful employment", mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", new.mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(new.mn.emp.record == "MN emp record", "MN emp record - not meaningful", new.mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(mn.emp.record == "No MN emp record", "No MN emp record", new.mn.emp.record),
         meaningful.emp.code = ifelse(new.mn.emp.record == "Meaningful employment", 1, 0)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  filter(meaningful.emp.code == max(meaningful.emp.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  distinct(PersonID, grad.year, meaningful.emp.code, .keep_all = TRUE)

Now, we want to determine if the locations of meaningful employment match the counties and regions from which they graduated high school. To do this, we will import the latest master dataset so we can compare their high school locations with meaningful employment locations.


emp.original.locations <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4)),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Shakopee Mdewakanton Community", "Scott"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen")) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions.1, by = c("CountyName" = "Name")) %>%
  select(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, EconomicDevelopmentRegionName, CountyName, project.pr) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, EconomicDevelopmentRegionName, CountyName, project.pr) %>%
  rename(employment.county = CountyName,
         emp.edr = EconomicDevelopmentRegionName,
         emp.pr = project.pr) %>%
  mutate(emp.edr = str_replace(emp.edr, "  ", " "),
         emp.edr = as.factor(emp.edr),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, " County", ""),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen"),
         employment.county = as.factor(employment.county)) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions[,c(2,4)], by = c("employment.county" = "Name")) %>%
  rename(emp.Dem_Desc = Dem_Desc) 

meaningful.emp.locations <- meaningful.employer %>%
  left_join(emp.original.locations, by = c("PersonID", "CalendarYear", "EmploymentOrganizationID")) %>%
  mutate(emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)", "Unknown", as.character(emp.edr)),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)", "Unknown", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Hennepin", "EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Ramsey", "EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "St. Louis", "EDR 3 - Arrowhead", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Unknown", "Unknown", emp.edr),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "Unknown", "Unknown", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "NULL", "NULL", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Mahnomen", "EDR 2 - Headwaters", emp.edr))

grad.locations <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-10.csv") %>%
  filter(hs.grad.year < 2024) %>%

grad.emp.location.match <- grad.locations %>%
  left_join(meaningful.emp.locations, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(county.match = new.mn.emp.record,
         new.county.match = ifelse(county.match == "Meaningful employment" & employment.county == hs.county.name, "Meaningful emp - match", county.match),
         new.county.match = ifelse(new.county.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - no match", new.county.match),
         new.county.match = fct_relevel(new.county.match, "Meaningful emp - match", "Meaningful emp - no match", "MN emp record - not meaningful", "No MN emp record", "After 2023")) %>%
  select(-county.match) %>%
  rename(county.match = new.county.match) %>%
  mutate(edr.match = new.mn.emp.record,
         new.edr.match = ifelse(edr.match == "Meaningful employment" & emp.edr == hs.edr, "Meaningful emp - match", edr.match),
         new.edr.match = ifelse(new.edr.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - no match", new.edr.match),
         new.edr.match = fct_relevel(new.edr.match, "Meaningful emp - match", "Meaningful emp - no match", "MN emp record - not meaningful", "No MN emp record", "After 2023")) %>%
  select(-edr.match) %>%
  rename(edr.match = new.edr.match) %>%
  mutate(region.match = new.mn.emp.record,
         new.region.match = ifelse(region.match == "Meaningful employment" & emp.pr %in% c("Southwest"), "Meaningful emp - match", region.match),
         new.region.match = ifelse(new.region.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - no match", new.region.match),
         new.region.match = fct_relevel(new.region.match, "Meaningful emp - match", "Meaningful emp - no match", "MN emp record - not meaningful", "No MN emp record", "After 2023")) %>%
  select(-region.match) %>%
  rename(region.match = new.region.match) %>%
  mutate(state.match = new.mn.emp.record,
         new.state.match = ifelse(!is.na(emp.edr) & state.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - match",
                                  ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)" & state.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - match", state.match)),
         new.state.match = fct_relevel(new.state.match, "Meaningful emp - match", "MN emp record - not meaningful", "No MN emp record", "After 2023")) %>%
  select(-state.match) %>%
  rename(state.match = new.state.match) %>%
  mutate(Dem_Desc.match = new.mn.emp.record,
         new.Dem_Desc.match = ifelse(Dem_Desc.match == "Meaningful employment" & hs.Dem_Desc == emp.Dem_Desc, "Meaningful emp - match", Dem_Desc.match),
         new.Dem_Desc.match = ifelse(new.Dem_Desc.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - no match", new.Dem_Desc.match),
         new.Dem_Desc.match = fct_relevel(new.Dem_Desc.match, "Meaningful emp - match", "Meaningful emp - no match", "MN emp record - not meaningful", "No MN emp record", "After 2023")) %>%
  select(-Dem_Desc.match) %>%
  rename(Dem_Desc.match = new.Dem_Desc.match) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, grad.year, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(PersonID, hs.grad.year, grad.year, county.match, edr.match, region.match, Dem_Desc.match, state.match)

This dataset has 32,460 rows and 6 columns. Here are explanations of the rows:

Graduated: Whether the student graduated. This dataset only provides students that have a “Y” in the column.
GraduationTimeID: Provides the yearmonthday of the PersonID graduation.
OPEID: ID of the institution which has been converted to an 8 long string padded with “0” on the left.
InstitutionName: Name of the institution from which the PersonID graduated.
DegreeTitle: The Degree Title the PersonID graduated with. This column is a shitshow - some have values of BA, while others have it written out - Bachelor of Arts. I will need to fix this.
Major - Major the PersonID graduated with.
OPEID.6 - this is the OPEID with a string length of 6 so that it matches up with our IPEDS dataset.

The main characteristics from this dataset that I want to add to the master dataset/model are the following;

Confirmation that they graduated from a post secondary institution
The year they graduated from their first post secondary institution
The year they graduated from their last post-seconary institution
The sector of the institution(s) from which they graduated
The highest level of degree obtained by the PersonID
The degrees earned
Whether the institution(s) from which they graduated are in the same RUCA category, EDR, planning region, and state as their high school

Okay, lets first create a dataset with a unique PersonID and a column confirming that they graduated from a post secondary institution. However, we don’t want to include any students that never had a chance to complete their post-secondary institution. For example, if an individual has graduated by 2023 (the last year of the data), but is attending, then they shouldn’t be counted against the region for not having that person not “graduated”.
Essentially, what we want to identify is that in 2023, has the individual;

Graduated from a post-secondary institution,
Is still attending post-secondary institution,
Not attending post-secondary and never graduated from one.

To do this, I will need to import the NSC enrollment data, filter to 2023, and double check to see if anyone in our graduate list was attending post-secondary that year. Then ps.grad can be categorized as the following;

ps.grad: graduated from a post-secondary institution by 2023
ps.attending: attending post-secondary as of 2023
not.ps.grad: never graduated from a post-secondary institution and wasn’t enrolled in one as of 2023.



ps.enrollment <- read_csv('/Users/kellyasche/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY27/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/CRPD 2 (angelique.workman@state.mn.us)/NSC_Enrollments.csv') %>%
  mutate(PersonID = as.integer(PersonID),
         OPEID = str_pad(OPEID, width = 8, side = "left", pad = "0"),
         OPEID.6 = str_sub(OPEID, 1, 6)) %>%
  drop_na(PersonID) %>%
  drop_na(OPEID) %>%
  filter(!EnrollmentStatus %in% c("A", "W", "D")) %>%
  mutate(enrollment.year = str_sub(EnrollmentEndTimeID, 1,4),
         enrollment.year = as.integer(enrollment.year)) %>%
  filter(enrollment.year == 2023) %>%
  select(PersonID, enrollment.year) %>%
  mutate(ps.attending.2023 = "Yes") %>%
  select(-enrollment.year) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE)

Next we will determine the sector(s) of the institution(s) from which they graduated. If they graduated from multiple institutions with different sectors than a new category will be created defined as “Graduated from multiple institution sectors”. This will be coded as “10”. I will use the IPEDS sector data. Here are the definitions of the institution sector;

0 - Administrative Unit

1 - Public, 4-year or above

2 - Private not-for-profit, 4-year or above

3 - Private for-profit, 4-year or above

4 - Public, 2-year

5 - Private not-for-profit, 2-year

6 - Private for-profit, 2-year

7 - Public, less-than 2-year

8 - Private not-for-profit, less-than 2-year

9 - Private for-profit, less-than 2-year

10 - Multiple sectors
99 - Sector unknown (not active)

  mutate(credential.code = as.factor(credential.code)) %>%
  mutate(cred.level = ifelse(credential.code %in% c("CR", "PD", "UC"), "Less than Associate Degree",

  distinct(PersonID, cred.level.code, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%

master.10 <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-9.csv") %>%
  mutate(PersonID = as.integer(PersonID)) %>%

  left_join(ps.enrollment, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(new.Graduated = ifelse(is.na(Graduated) & ps.attending.2023 == "Yes", "Attending ps",

         new.Graduated = ifelse(is.na(Graduated) & is.na(ps.attending.2023), "No", new.Graduated)) %>%

  left_join(year.first.last.graduated, by = "PersonID") %>%

title: Dependent Variables States
text:
master.original <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/After analysis/Master-final-after-mca.csv") 


There are many paths in which an individual can take after graduating high school. What we are most concerned with is whether an individual has “meaningful” employment, when and where this employment takes place, and are there any variables that are associated with each of these pathways.
The paths that we want to identify are the following;

Meaningful employment

Meaningful employment - same county as high school
Meaningful employment - same EDR/region as high school, but not the same county
Meaningful employment - in Minnesota, but not in Central Minnesota

Not meaningful employment or no MN Employment record - attending post-secondary
Not meaningful employment - not attending post-secondary
No MN employment record - not attending post-secondary

We are going to assess each PersonID on which of those pathways they are at the time of their high school graduation, and each subsequent year up to 2023.
We have already created the employment states for each year.

The dataset has 311,408 rows and 6 columns. Here are the columns and their definitions.

EnrollmentBeginTimeID: Begin date for the student’s period of attendance.
EnrollmentEndTimeID: End date for the student’s period of attendance.
OPEID: Office of Postsecondary Education (OPE)/FICE code of the college that the student attended (Foreign Key to IPEDSCharacteristics).
InstitutionName: Name of institution
EnrollmentStatus: The last enrollment status reported for the student. This field will have ‘N/A’ or “NULL” if the reporting college has not defined the student’s enrollment status as directory information. Here are the code definitions;

F: Full-time
Q: Three-quarter time
H: Half-time
L: Less than half-time
A: Leave of absence
W: Withdrawn
D: Deceased


Essentially, this dataset provides semester-based information - each observation is a semester/single period with the institutional information and beginning and end time of that single period (usually a semester). For example, if an individual attended South Dakota State University, attended in a “typical” fashion (fall and spring semesters), and graduated in 4 years, there would be 8 observations for that PersonID - one observation per semester.
The primary pieces of information I want from this dataset is each year a PersonID was attending a post-secondary institution. So let’s shrink the dataset down to just the following columns;

PersonID
unique year attending a post-secondary institution

The PersonID will be filtered using the EnrollmentStatus variable equaling full-time, three-quarter time, half-time, and less than half-time.
For the unique year, it won’t matter how many semesters they were attending. If an individual attended half a year, then worked full-time, my meaningful employment definition should pick it up and transfer it into that category. Otherwise, they will be in the category - attending post-secondary with no meaningful employment or no MN employment record.

         end.year = str_sub(EnrollmentEndTimeID, 1, 4)) %>%
  select(PersonID, begin.year, end.year) %>%
  gather(key = "BeginOrEnd", value = "year", 2:3) %>%
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, year) %>%
  rename(ps.attend.year = year) %>%
  mutate(ps.attend = "ps.attend")

The new dataset has 813,280 rows and 10 with 50,830 unique individuals. The seven states are labeled as the following;

Meaningful emp County: means they have worked 1,000 hours or more for one employer located in the same county as their high school.
Meaningful emp region: means they have worked 1,000 hours or more for one employer located in Southwest Minnesota.
Meaningful emp MN - means they have worked 1,000 hours or more for one employer located in Minnesota, but not in Southwest Minnesota.
Attending ps: Means the individuals either has a MN employment record but it isn’t meaningful OR they do not have a MN employment record, but they are attending post-secondary.
Not meaningful, not attending ps: this means they do have a MN employment record, but it isn’t meaningful and they are not attending post-secondary.
No MN emp record - not attending ps: this means they do not have a MN employment record nor are they attending a post-secondary institution.

The other designation is “After 2023” which will be filtered out whenever I analyze the dataset.
Let’s first take a look at the proportion of individuals that are in each state at each grad.year.x.
The chart below shows the proportion of individuals in the dataset that are in each “state/path” for each grad.year.x. There are a couple of things to highlight.

The percentage of individuals with meaningful employment in Southwest Minnesota peaks about 6 years after college with nearly 25% of graduates working 1,000 hours or more that year for a single employer.
At 6 years after graduating, nearly half of the graduates have meaningful employment in Minnesota.
Graduates not reaching the meaningful employment threshold in Minnesota hovers around 15% after the first year of graduating high school.
Over a third of graduates disappear from my dataset about 10 years after graduating. This means they are not going to post-secondary in the United States and do not have a Minnesota employment record.



prop.states <- seven.states %>%
  filter(states != "After 2023") %>%
  group_by(grad.year, states) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(grad.year) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(data_id = seq(n())) %>%
  group_by(grad.year) %>%
  arrange(desc(states)) %>%
  mutate(cum.pct = cumsum(pct),
         x.loc = cum.pct - ((cum.pct - lag(cum.pct)) / 2),
         x.loc = ifelse(states == "No MN emp record, not attending ps", cum.pct/2, x.loc)) %>%
  ungroup()

seven.states.plot <- ggplot(prop.states, aes(as.numeric(grad.year)-1, pct, fill = states, group = states)) +
  geom_area_interactive(aes(data_id = data_id, tooltip = paste("State: ", states, "\n", percent(pct, accuracy = .1), sep = ""))) +
  geom_label_repel(data = filter(prop.states, grad.year %in% c("grad.year.0", "grad.year.6", "grad.year.11")), aes(x = as.numeric(grad.year)-1, y = x.loc, label = paste(grad.year, "\n", percent(pct, accuracy = .1))), show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(x="Grad Year", y = "Proportion of individuals", color="", title = "Percent share of path by grad year X")+
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent)+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 20, 2)) +
  theme_bar+
  scale_fill_manual(values = brewer.pal(n = 7, "RdYlBu"),
                    guide = guide_legend(ncol = 2)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        text = element_text(size = 18))


girafe(ggobj = seven.states.plot, width_svg = 10, height_svg = 10) %>%
  girafe_options(opts_selection(type = "none"),
                 opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE))
