title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
text:
Model 4 — Year 10: Adding Post-secondary Attendance
Overview Model 4 adds attended.ps to the full Model 3 specification, maintaining the same sample of 11,448 non-college completers. VIF values remained well below 2.0 for all predictors including attended.ps (GVIF^(1/(2*Df))=1.03), indicating no multicollinearity concerns. The addition of this variable produces negligible improvement in model fit (ΔAIC=-1.42, Nagelkerke R²=0.051, essentially unchanged from Model 3), consistent with the bivariate finding that postsecondary attendance’s influence is short-lived rather than durable.
Stability and Attenuation of Previous Coefficients Most Model 3 coefficients remain stable with the addition of attended.ps. - Economic status becomes significant for the first time at any stage of this analysis (OR from 0.915, p=.057 to 0.909, 95% CI [0.830, 0.996], p=.040), a new finding that emerges only once postsecondary attendance is isolated as its own term - Gender, race/ethnicity, Dem_Desc, EDR, average unemployment rate, CTE achievement, and MCA Reading all remain essentially unchanged from Model 3
Postsecondary Attendance A marginal, not quite statistically significant negative association with regional employment (OR=0.920, 95% CI [0.842, 1.005], p=.064). This represents a genuine sign reversal, not merely attenuation, from the strong positive association observed at year 1 (OR=1.692, p<.001) and the smaller positive association at year 5 (OR=1.059, p=.087). By year 10, non-completers who attended postsecondary trend toward lower, not higher, odds of regional employment relative to those who never attended — the opposite of the pattern observed immediately after high school.
Summary The addition of postsecondary attendance produces no meaningful improvement in model fit at year 10, confirming the bivariate finding that its influence is concentrated in the immediate post-graduation period. Unlike years 1 and 5, however, its coefficient does not simply fade toward zero — it crosses into negative territory, suggesting that non-completers who attempted but did not finish postsecondary education may face a modest long-term disadvantage in regional employment relative to those who entered the workforce directly, a pattern worth further investigation given it runs counter to the variable’s dominant early-career role. This is the full confirmatory specification for year 10: MCA Reading and average unemployment rate have both grown into the strongest independent associates of regional employment by this stage, CTE achievement remains significant though increasingly attenuated, and Dem_Desc’s urban penalty persists as the most stable finding across the entire three-time-point analysis.

title: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis - Non-college grads
section: Multivariate Confirmation Analysis Summary — Non-College Completers in Northwest Minnesota
text:
Multivariate Confirmation Analysis Summary — Non-College Completers in Northwest Minnesota
CTE Engagement Is the Most Consistent and Durable Associate
CTE achievement is the only high school accomplishment variable that shows a significant, stable, positive association with regional employment at all three time points and in every model specification. CTE Concentrators or Completors show odds of regional employment roughly 50-70% higher than No CTE non-completers across the full ten-year window (final model OR=1.695 at year 1, OR=1.591 at year 5, OR=1.507 at year 10), with CTE Participants showing a smaller but similarly durable positive association throughout. While the magnitude attenuates modestly over time, CTE never loses significance and never changes direction — the only variable in this analysis with that distinction. This confirms CTE as the central, policy-actionable mechanism connecting high school preparation to long-term regional workforce retention among non-completers.
Post-Secondary Attendance and Academic Proficiency Shift Direction Over Time
Two variables show genuine sign reversals across the ten-year window rather than simple attenuation. Attended post-secondary is the dominant predictor at year 1 (OR=1.692, p<.001) — the largest single association in the entire year 1 sequence — but weakens to marginal non-significance by year 5 (OR=1.059, p=.087) and crosses into negative territory by year 10 (OR=0.920, p=.064). This is not fading toward null; it is a reversal, suggesting non-completers who attempted postsecondary education without finishing may carry a modest long-term disadvantage relative to those who entered the workforce directly, despite an initial advantage.
MCA Reading shows the opposite trajectory — a monotonic strengthening rather than a reversal. It shows no independent association at year 1 (p=.075, marginal), becomes significant at year 5 (OR=0.938, p=.001), and shows its strongest effect at year 10 (OR=0.850, p<.001). This confirms academic proficiency as an increasingly powerful predictor of out-of-region mobility the further out from high school graduation one looks — the opposite pattern from attended post-secondary’s declining relevance.
Local Labor Market Context Becomes Increasingly Important Over Time
Average county unemployment rate shows the clearest monotonic pattern in the entire analysis, strengthening steadily across all three time points and every model specification: non-significant at year 1 (OR=0.994, p=.658), significant at year 5 (OR=1.028, p=.016), and most strongly significant at year 10 (OR=1.102, p<.001). This provides increasingly strong confirmation of the North Dakota cross-border employment interpretation established in the bivariate analysis — individuals with no Minnesota employment record are concentrated in lower-unemployment border counties, and this pattern becomes more pronounced, not less, as more time passes since graduation. Average wages as a percent of state, by contrast, is significant only at year 1 (OR=1.923, p=.015) and non-significant at years 5 and 10, suggesting county wage levels matter for immediate post-graduation decisions but not for longer-term attachment.
The Urban Penalty Is Structural, Persistent, and Growing
Dem_Desc’s entirely-urban penalty is the single most stable and deepening finding in this analysis. Entirely urban non-completers show significantly lower odds of regional employment relative to entirely rural non-completers at every time point and every model specification, with the penalty growing steadily more severe: OR=0.628 at year 1, OR=0.487 at year 5, OR=0.470 at year 10 (final model estimates). Unlike nearly every other variable examined, this association shows no meaningful attenuation once high school accomplishments, local labor market context, or postsecondary attendance are controlled — confirming that community type operates as an independent, structural mechanism rather than a proxy for demographic or preparation differences.
Gender Disparities Are Persistent and Structural
Females show significantly lower odds of regional employment than males at every time point and every model specification, with the gap widening slightly over time (final model OR=0.869 at year 1, OR=0.802 at year 5, OR=0.795 at year 10). The consistency and modest strengthening of this disparity, net of community type, CTE engagement, academic preparation, and local labor market context, is consistent with the bivariate interpretation that it reflects the male-dominated industry composition of the Northwest Minnesota regional economy rather than a preparation or access gap.
Racial and Ethnic Disparities Persist Net of All Variables
Racial and ethnic patterns vary considerably by group and by time point, in contrast to the more uniform demographic patterns above. Asian/PI non-completers show a significant disadvantage at every time point, growing to the largest disparity observed anywhere in this analysis by year 10 (OR=0.352). Black non-completers show a marginal association at year 1 that strengthens to a stable, significant disparity by years 5 and 10 (final model OR≈0.52 at both stages). Hispanic non-completers show a significant disparity at year 5 only, with non-significant associations at years 1 and 10. AI non-completers show no significant association at any time point or model specification — a pattern distinct from the full-population and postsecondary-completer analyses, where AI disparities were consistently among the largest observed. The persistence of Black and Asian/PI disparities net of community type, CTE engagement, academic preparation, and postsecondary attendance indicates structural barriers to regional employment that are not explained by the mechanisms examined in this analysis.
Other Structural Variables Shift Over Time
Special education status, economic status, PSEO participation, and EDR each show unstable or time-limited patterns rather than consistent trajectories. Special education status is significantly associated with lower regional employment odds at years 1 and 5 (final model OR=0.836 and OR=0.908 respectively) but becomes non-significant by year 10, and shows notable instability across model specifications within the year 10 sequence specifically — significant positive in the demographic baseline, then non-significant once academic preparation is controlled — suggesting its early disadvantage resolves over time through mechanisms only partially captured by the variables in this model. Economic status shows no significant association at years 1 or 5 but becomes significant at year 10 only once postsecondary attendance is isolated as its own term (OR=0.909, p=.040), a delayed and unexpected finding. PSEO participation shows a significant negative association at years 1 and 5 that fully resolves to non-significance by year 10. EDR shows no significant association at year 1, a significant Headwaters disadvantage at year 5 that persists only through Model 2 before attenuating, and no significant association in the final year 10 model — the weakest and least stable predictor examined, consistent with its identification as one of the two weakest bivariate predictors overall.
Overall Conclusion
Across the ten-year window examined, three findings stand out as the most robust and policy-relevant. First, CTE engagement is the only mechanism examined that shows a consistently positive, significant, and durable association with regional employment at every stage — the clearest and most actionable lever for regional workforce retention among non-college completers. Second, community type operates as a persistent and deepening structural factor independent of preparation, academic proficiency, or postsecondary exposure, with entirely urban non-completers facing a growing regional employment penalty over time. Third, the mechanisms shaping regional attachment shift substantially across the decade: early-career outcomes are dominated by postsecondary attendance status and CTE engagement, while longer-term outcomes are increasingly shaped by academic proficiency (in a direction that favors out-of-region mobility) and local labor market context, particularly the North Dakota cross-border employment pattern. This time-varying structure confirms that a single cross-sectional model would have substantially mischaracterized the mechanisms driving regional workforce attachment among non-college completers, and that policy interventions calibrated to the immediate post-graduation period — such as those targeting postsecondary transition support — may need to be paired with distinct, longer-horizon strategies addressing local economic opportunity and CTE-pathway investment to sustain regional retention over the full first decade of the workforce.

We have 6,198,938 rows and 5 columns in this dataset. Here are the descriptions for each of the columns.

K12AsstTimeID: Day, month, and year the assessment took place.
TestName: Name of the test taken. There are 12 different tests in the dataset -

ACCESS: English proficiency,
ALTACCESS: English proficiency for special education or meet requirements
MCA-II & MCA-III: Minnesota Comprehsensive Assessments (series 2 and 3)
MOD-II, MOD-III: Modified Comprehensive Assessment, used only until 2014
MTAS & MTAS-III: Minnesota Test of Academic Skills
MTELL: an alternate assessment for students learning English (like the MTAS or MOD). MTELL was only administered from 2007-2010 during the series-II of MCAs.
SOLOM: Minnesota Student Oral Language Observation Matrix
TEAE: one of two assessments that Minnesota used to meet the requirements to test ELs in all four domains of language (the other was SOLOM). TEAE was used 2002 until we changed to ACCESS in 2012. SOLOM was used 2004 until we changed to ACCESS in 2012.

Subject: Classifies each test that is given to a student based on the areas measured. There are 8 factors;

A: Aural (listening) - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
C: Composite - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
L: Listening/Speaking
M: Math
O: Oral - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
R: Reading
S: Science
W: Writing

GradeTested: Grade student was enrolled in when performing assessment.
AchievementLevel: Used to count the number of students in each achievement level by group such as race, gender, and ethnicity. It must be calculated from other students at a similar graden and subject for a specific year.

ACCESS students are graded on a language proficiency scale of 1 through 6.
ALT-ACCESS students are graded using a P1 through P3 and A1 through A3 scale.
There are 4 different levels for the MCA test

D: Does not meet standards
E: Exceeds standards
M: Meets Standards
P: Partially meets standards

SOLOM tests are 1-5 scale with 5 being the highest
TEAE tests are 1-5 scale with 5 being the highest.


There are two ways in which we are going to code our graduates.
The first is to identify whether a student has been identified as an English learner. This means filtering students that have taken the ACCESS, ALT-ACCESS, MTELL, MTAS, TEAE, MOD-II, MOD-III, or SOLOM at least once in their career.
The second is be determining their highest achievement level in each subject of the MCA tests within the dataset. The dataset provides each instance of a test for each student so many are students are listed numerous times - once for each time they took a test.
Lets do this in two separate files and then join each with the master file.
Starting with identifying the EL students.


el <- assessments.original %>%
  filter(!TestName %in% c("MCA-II", "MCA-III")) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(english.learner = 1)

This dataset identified 37,906 individuals who were identified as an english learner at least one time in the original dataset.
Now we will determine the highest achievement level for each subject for each student.


mca <- assessments.original %>%
  filter(TestName %in% c("MCA-II", "MCA-III")) %>%
  filter(AchievementLevel != "NULL") %>%
  droplevels() %>%
  mutate(AchievementLevelCode = ifelse(AchievementLevel == "D", 1,
                                       ifelse(AchievementLevel == "P", 2,
                                              ifelse(AchievementLevel == "M", 3, 4))))

mca.highest <- mca %>%
  group_by(PersonID, Subject) %>%
  filter(AchievementLevelCode == max(AchievementLevelCode)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(PersonID, Subject, AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  mutate(mca.subject = paste("MCA.", Subject, sep = "")) %>%
  select(PersonID, mca.subject, AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  mutate(id = seq(n())) %>%
  spread(key = mca.subject, value = AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  fill(MCA.M, .direction = c("downup")) %>%
  fill(MCA.R, .direction = "downup") %>%
  fill(MCA.S, .direction = "downup") %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(-id)

There seems to be a minor coding error in the careercluster column. For one particular class, it was consistently labeled “Information Technology” even though the field requires a number value. In addition, “information Technology” doesn’t seem to match the course due to the following information;
Program Course Name: Family and Consumer Science Course title: Apparrel CareerCluster: Design CareerClusterName: 6 (which should be a letter value, not a code).
Due to this information, I recoded anything that was “Information Technology” for that particular course as a “6”.
In addition, there were some errors in careercluster 26, which is supposed to be “Administrative only” but had a number of “Youth Apprenticeships” in it that I recoded to CareerCluster 25.

section: Summary - Number of CTE courses taken by a student
text:
Summary - Number of CTE courses taken by a student

We’ll start with summarising the number of cte courses the observations have taken.


cte.n.courses.summary.total <- master.4 %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(total.cte.courses.taken),
            median = median(total.cte.courses.taken),
            sd = sd(total.cte.courses.taken),
            n = comma(n(), accuracy = 1),
            min = min(total.cte.courses.taken),
            max = max(total.cte.courses.taken)) %>%
  mutate(population = "All graduates",
         mean = comma(mean, accuracy = .01),
         sd = comma(sd, accuracy = .01))

cte.n.courses.summary.ctestudents <- master.4 %>%
  filter(total.cte.courses.taken > 0) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(total.cte.courses.taken),
            median = median(total.cte.courses.taken),
            sd = sd(total.cte.courses.taken),
            n = comma(n(), accuracy = 1),
            min = min(total.cte.courses.taken),
            max = max(total.cte.courses.taken)) %>%
  mutate(population = "Only graduates with CTE courses > 0",
         mean = comma(mean, accuracy = .01),
         sd = comma(sd, accuracy = .01))
  
cte.n.courses.summary.total.ctestudents <- cte.n.courses.summary.total %>%
  rbind(cte.n.courses.summary.ctestudents) %>%
  select(population, n, mean, median, sd, min, max)

datatable(cte.n.courses.summary.total.ctestudents, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top")

  labs(x="", y = "", color="", title = "Histogram - N CTE courses")+
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::comma)+
  theme_line+
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        text = element_text(size = 16))

title: CTEEnrollment
section: Summary - CareerCluster of CTE courses taken
text:
Summary - CareerCluster of CTE courses taken
Let’s dig into the breadth of CTE course concentrations a graduate would take by looking at the proportion of graduates that took at least one course within a concentration.


cte.cf.prop <- master.4 %>%
  gather(key = "CareerCluster", value = "n.courses", `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  mutate(cte.cf.taken = ifelse(n.courses > 0, "Yes", "No")) %>%
  tabyl(CareerCluster, cte.cf.taken) %>%
  mutate(pct.taken.cf = Yes / (Yes + No)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(pct.taken.cf))

datatable(cte.cf.prop, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(scrollX = TRUE)) %>%
  formatCurrency(2:3, "", digits = 0) %>%
  formatPercentage(4)






Now we will take a look at the breakdown of the number of times a CTE courses has been taken within a CareerCluster for each PersonID. I expect there to be a lot of variation in this data since different schools might focus on different types of CTE offerings depending on the local employment makeup.


cte.cf.concentration.total <- master.4 %>%
  select(PersonID,  `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  gather(key = "CareerCluster", value = "n.courses", 2:ncol(.)) %>%
  group_by(CareerCluster) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(n.courses)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(pct = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = .1)) %>%
  arrange(CareerCluster)

  datatable(cte.cf.concentration.total, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE)






Lets see how this looks broken down by county.


cte.cf.concentration.county <- master.4 %>%
  select(PersonID, county.name, countyfp,  `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  gather(key = "CareerCluster", value = "n.courses",  `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  group_by(county.name, countyfp, CareerCluster) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(n.courses)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(county.name, countyfp) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename(CareerClusterName = CareerCluster) %>%
  left_join(mn_counties[,c(5,7)], by = "countyfp")

cte.cf.concentration.county.map <- ggplot(data = filter(cte.cf.concentration.county, pct > .05)) +
  facet_wrap(~CareerClusterName, ncol = 2,
             labeller = label_wrap_gen(15)) +
  geom_sf_interactive(color = "grey85", aes(geometry = geometry, fill = pct, data_id = countyfp, tooltip = paste(county.name, "\nCareerCluster: ", CareerClusterName, "\nPercent of courses taken in this CareerCluster: ", percent(pct, accuracy = .1), sep = ""))) +
  theme_sf+
  scale_fill_fermenter(palette = "PuBu", direction = 1, labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = str_wrap("Percent of CTE courses taken within each CareerCluster by county", 39)) +
  theme(legend.box.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0),
        text = element_text(size = 16),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 8))

girafe(ggobj = cte.cf.concentration.county.map, height_svg = 20) %>%
  girafe_options(opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE))






The next big question is whether these percentages vary by year. Are there any trends?


cte.cf.concentration.year <- master.4 %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.year, `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  gather(key = "CareerCluster", value = "n.courses", `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  group_by(grad.year, CareerCluster) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(n.courses)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(grad.year) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(grad.year > 2006) %>%
  mutate(data_id = seq(n())) %>%
  rename(CareerClusterName = CareerCluster) 


cte.cf.concentration.year.plot <- ggplot(cte.cf.concentration.year, aes(grad.year, pct, color = CareerClusterName)) +
  geom_point_interactive(size = 3, aes(data_id = data_id, tooltip = paste(CareerClusterName, "\nYear: ", grad.year, "\nCareerCluster: ", CareerClusterName, "\nPercent of CTE courses taken: ", percent(pct, accuracy = .1), sep = ""))) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x="", y = "", color="", title = "Percent of taken CTE courses")+
  geom_label(data = filter(cte.cf.concentration.year, grad.year == max(cte.cf.concentration.year$grad.year)), aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = .1)), show.legend = FALSE, size = 5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent)+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1900, 2050, 2),
                     guide = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2)) +
  theme_line+
  scale_color_discrete(guide = guide_legend(ncol = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        text = element_text(size = 14))

  girafe(ggobj = cte.cf.concentration.year.plot, width_svg = 10, height_svg = 7) %>%
    girafe_options(opts_selection(type = "none"),
                   opts_toolbar(saveaspng = FALSE),
                   opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE))

title: Pathways After High School – Southwest Minnesota
text:
After extensive analysis examining relationships between individual and independent variables, and workforce participation outcomes, the following pathways are clear.



This pathway is defined by postsecondary credential attainment, and the most important variable within it is not whether someone completes college but where they complete it. The ps.pathway variable in the full population multivariate analysis made this unmistakably clear — graduating from a regional institution, whether with a sub-baccalaureate or bachelor’s degree, is the single strongest postsecondary predictor of regional workforce retention (OR≈2.0 for both regional graduation categories). Graduating from a non-regional Minnesota institution or outside Minnesota is associated with dramatically lower regional employment odds.
The variables that predict whether someone reaches this pathway are well established — female gender, higher academic achievement (ACT, MCA scores, AP participation), non-disadvantaged economic status, and non-special education status all increase postsecondary graduation likelihood substantially. Economic status and special education status are the two largest barriers, each producing odds of postsecondary graduation below 0.40 in the full population baseline model.
The key tension within this pathway for regional workforce policy is that the variables that most reliably produce college completers — high academic achievement, ACT participation, AP exposure — are the same variables most associated with non-regional graduation and non-regional employment. The pipeline that produces credentials exports them.



This is the CTE pathway, and it is the most analytically clean finding in the entire project. Among non-college completers, total CTE courses taken shows an odds ratio of approximately 1.055 for sustained regional employment at year 1, year 5, and year 10 — a stability that no other variable in the analysis approaches. CTE achievement level produces similarly consistent associations, with concentrators showing nearly double the regional employment rates of no-CTE graduates by year 5.
The key variables within this pathway are:

Total CTE courses taken is the dominant predictor — dose-dependent, durable, and independent of every other variable in the model. More courses means more regional employment, period, across a decade of observation.
CTE achievement level adds categorical confirmation of the dose-response pattern — concentrators outperform participants who outperform no-CTE graduates at every time point.
Gender operates within this pathway in an important way — males are substantially more likely to achieve sustained regional employment through the workforce-first route, and the gender gap widens over time. Whether this reflects differential access to certain CTE program areas, differential regional employer preferences, or differential geographic mobility among female non-completers, the data cannot fully resolve.
EDR and local labor market conditions matter within this pathway more than elsewhere — graduates from higher-unemployment counties show lower regional employment odds at year 1 and year 10, suggesting that the workforce-first pathway is more accessible in some subregions than others, and that CTE engagement cannot fully overcome severe local labor market constraints.
Special education status deserves specific attention within this pathway. Special education graduates are more likely to be CTE-engaged and less academically oriented, which initially appears to favor regional employment. But once CTE engagement and academic achievement are controlled, special education graduates show lower regional employment odds — suggesting barriers to sustained regional employment that CTE engagement alone does not fully overcome.




This is the most important and least well-understood pathway in the analysis. It is also the largest — the modal experience among non-college completers is persistent disconnection, with 50.4% disconnected in four or five of their first five post-exit years, and the no MN employment record category growing from 28.8% at year 1 to nearly 39% by year 10.
The variables associated with this pathway are less a set of positive predictors and more an absence of the protective factors that define the other two pathways:
No CTE engagement is the single strongest predictor of disconnection — no-CTE graduates show nearly 48% no MN employment record rates by year 5, nearly double the rate of CTE concentrators. The disconnected pathway is in many ways defined by the absence of CTE.
No academic orientation means these graduates also lack the college preparedness signals that route others toward postsecondary or statewide employment. They are neither anchored by CTE nor oriented by academic preparation — they fall between both pathways.
Demographic concentration matters here in ways it does not in the other pathways. American Indian graduates show 40-47% no MN employment record rates at every annual time point regardless of high school experiences. English learner graduates show elevated and growing absence from Minnesota records. Female non-completers increasingly accumulate in this category over time. Black graduates show persistent no MN record rates that survive all multivariate controls. These are not simply the product of lower CTE engagement or lower academic achievement — they reflect structural barriers that the data identify but cannot fully explain.
The two disconnection signatures identified in the annual analysis are critically important for understanding this pathway’s internal heterogeneity. Local underutilization — elevated in-region marginal employment among SpEd graduates, economically disadvantaged graduates, low-CTE graduates — is a different problem from geographic absence — elevated no MN record among EL graduates, AI graduates, female graduates, higher achievers. These two groups are both in the disconnected pathway but for fundamentally different reasons, and they require fundamentally different interventions.



What makes these three pathways analytically powerful is that they are not simply demographic categories — they are the product of a sequential sorting process that begins in high school and compounds over time. The variables that predict pathway membership are largely determined before graduation, and the data suggest that the sorting is largely irreversible within the observation window. Graduates who enter the disconnected pathway at year 1 are not meaningfully more likely to exit it by year 5 or year 10. The regional employment rates of CTE-engaged graduates are stable across a decade. The academic departure mechanism grows stronger over time rather than self-correcting.
This raises the most important policy question the data generate: if the sorting is largely complete by graduation, and if the disconnected pathway is the modal experience among non-college completers, then the intervention window is high school — and specifically the decision about whether and how deeply to engage students in CTE programming before they exit formal education entirely.

No academic orientation means these graduates also lack the college preparedness signals that route others toward postsecondary or statewide employment. They are neither anchored by CTE nor oriented by academic preparation — they fall between both pathways.
Demographic concentration matters here in ways it does not in the other pathways. American Indian graduates show 40-47% no MN employment record rates at every annual time point regardless of high school experiences. English learner graduates show elevated and growing absence from Minnesota records. Female non-completers increasingly accumulate in this category over time. Black graduates show persistent no MN record rates that survive all multivariate controls. These are not simply the product of lower CTE engagement or lower academic achievement — they reflect structural barriers that the data identify but cannot fully explain.
The two disconnection signatures identified in the annual analysis are critically important for understanding this pathway’s internal heterogeneity. Local underutilization — elevated in-region marginal employment among SpEd graduates, economically disadvantaged graduates, low-CTE graduates — is a different problem from geographic absence — elevated no MN record among EL graduates, AI graduates, female graduates, higher achievers. These two groups are both in the disconnected pathway but for fundamentally different reasons, and they require fundamentally different interventions.

title: Pathways After High School – Southwest Minnesota
text:
What makes these three pathways analytically powerful is that they are not simply demographic categories — they are the product of a sequential sorting process that begins in high school and compounds over time. The variables that predict pathway membership are largely determined before graduation, and the data suggest that the sorting is largely irreversible within the observation window. Graduates who enter the disconnected pathway at year 1 are not meaningfully more likely to exit it by year 5 or year 10. The regional employment rates of CTE-engaged graduates are stable across a decade. The academic departure mechanism grows stronger over time rather than self-correcting.
This raises the most important policy question the data generate: if the sorting is largely complete by graduation, and if the disconnected pathway is the modal experience among non-college completers, then the intervention window is high school — and specifically the decision about whether and how deeply to engage students in CTE programming before they exit formal education entirely.

The original dataset provides whether the student was a basic participant, basic concentrator, basic completor, and/or a centrentrator 150 when taking a CTE course. It looks like each observation is unique by grade of the student. This means that one PersonID can have multiple observations.
In order to determine how I want to organize this data so that each observation represents the full characteristics of each PersonID I need to understand how these values are defined.

Basic Participant: Any grade 9-12 student who successfully completes one or more state-approved CTE course(s).
Basic Concentrator: this is the old standard for years and required the student complete 240 hours. Any student successfully enrolled in a single CTE field for more than 240 hours (successful is defined as passing grade).
Basic Completor: any concentrator who attains academic and technical knowledge and skills and graduates from high school.
Concentrator 150: This is the new standard - Any grade 9-12 student who successfully completes 150+ course hours (or more) as part of a state-approved secondary CTE program, within one career field.

Judging by these definitions, it seems that we will want three categories;

Those that participated in a CTE course but were not a concentrator or a completor, and
Those that participated in a CTE course and graduated as a concentrator.
Those that did not participate in a CTE course.

So essentially, filtering this dataset to provide the “highest level achieved” in terms of CTE coursework. We will focus on filtering this dataset to the highest level achieved and will then join with the graduate list which will have all the individuals that did not participate in any CTE courses.


graduate <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-4.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID)

cte.concentrator.cat <- cte.demographics.original %>%
  gather(key = "cte.achievement", value = "yes.or.no", 4:7) %>%
  filter(yes.or.no != "Null") %>%
  filter(yes.or.no != "NULL") %>%
  filter(yes.or.no != "N") %>%
  mutate(cte.achievement = as.factor(cte.achievement),
         yes.or.no = as.factor(yes.or.no),
         cte.achievement.code = ifelse(cte.achievement == "BasicParticipant", 0, 1)) %>%
  select(PersonID, cte.achievement, cte.achievement.code) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarise(cte.achievement.code = sum(cte.achievement.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(cte.achievement = ifelse(cte.achievement.code == 0, "CTE Participant", "CTE Concentrator or Completor")) %>%
  select(PersonID, cte.achievement) %>%
  right_join(graduate, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(cte.achievement = ifelse(is.na(cte.achievement), "No CTE", cte.achievement))

As expected, we have 41,580 individuals in the dataset.


MCA analysis


Eigenvalues - Demographic Variables
Overview The MCA on demographic variables produced 9 dimensions, collectively explaining 100% of the variance in the data.
Dimension Retention Using the average eigenvalue threshold (1/k = 0.167), Dimensions 1-5 are recommended for retention, collectively explaining 74.6% of the total variance. Dimension 1 is clearly the strongest, explaining 27.8% of variance, with a notable drop-off to subsequent dimensions which each explain approximately 11%.
Notes The relatively even spread of variance across Dimensions 2-5 suggests that demographic variation in this dataset is multidimensional, with no single dominant second axis of variation.


demographics.mca <- FactoMineR::MCA(demographics, graph = FALSE)

eig.val <- get_eigenvalue(demographics.mca)

eig.val

      eigenvalue variance.percent cumulative.variance.percent
Dim.1  0.4174275         27.82850                    27.82850
Dim.2  0.1985924         13.23949                    41.06799
Dim.3  0.1705803         11.37202                    52.44001
Dim.4  0.1670065         11.13377                    63.57378
Dim.5  0.1660384         11.06923                    74.64301




COS2 - Demographic Variables
Overview COS2 measures the quality of representation of each variable category across the five retained dimensions. Values closer to 1 indicate that a category is well represented in the retained dimensional space.
Well Represented Categories Race/ethnicity categories are the best represented across the five dimensions. Black (0.970), Asian/PI (0.930), Hispanic (0.827), and AI (0.829) all show very strong representation, indicating these categories are well captured by the retained dimensions. The language variables non.english.home (0.823) and White (0.750) are also well represented.
Moderately Represented Categories SpecialEdStatus (0.661), english.learner (0.647), and Gender (0.611) show moderate representation, suggesting some variation in these variables extends beyond the five retained dimensions.
Weakest Represented Categories economic.status is the weakest represented variable at 0.437, suggesting that economic variation among students is not well captured by the five retained dimensions and may operate somewhat independently of other demographic factors.
Notes The expected symmetry between binary category pairs (e.g., economic.status_0 and economic.status_1) is present throughout, confirming the technical integrity of the MCA results.
<br>

table <- demographics.mca$var$cos2 %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  select(`Dim 1`, `Dim 2`, `Dim 3`, `Dim 4`, `Dim 5`) %>%
  mutate(total = `Dim 1` + `Dim 2` + `Dim 3` + `Dim 4` + `Dim 5`) 
  
datatable(table) %>%
  formatCurrency(1:6, "", digits = 3)




fviz_cos2(demographics.mca, choice = "var", axes = 1:5)











Contributions - Demographic Variables
Overview Contributions measure how much each variable category drives each retained dimension. Categories with higher contributions are the primary drivers of that dimension’s axis of variation.
Dimension 1 - English Language Learner / Hispanic Axis Dimension 1 is primarily driven by non.english.home_1 (27.2%), english.learner_1 (22.7%), and Hispanic (17.1%), indicating this axis captures variation among students who speak a non-English language at home, are English language learners, and are of Hispanic ethnicity. These three categories together account for over 67% of Dimension 1.
Dimension 2 - Special Education / Gender Axis Dimension 2 is dominated by SpecialEdStatus_1 (41.6%), with secondary contributions from Gender (F: 11.4%, M: 11.1%), suggesting this axis captures variation among students with special education status alongside an independent gender gradient.
Dimension 3 - American Indian / Gender Axis Dimension 3 is primarily driven by AI (48.9%) with notable secondary contributions from Gender (F: 14.3%, M: 14.0%), suggesting this axis captures variation unique to American Indian students alongside a gender gradient.
Dimension 4 - Multi-Minority Race/Ethnicity Axis Dimension 4 is shared across Black (33.8%), Hispanic (26.7%), and Asian/PI (19.1%) and AI (18.6%), suggesting this dimension captures a broader pattern of variation among minority race/ethnicity groups.
Dimension 5 - Black / Asian/PI Axis Dimension 5 is primarily driven by Black (46.6%) and Asian/PI (41.5%), suggesting this dimension captures residual variation that distinguishes these two groups from other minority race/ethnicity categories.
Notes The removal of unknown race/ethnicity individuals has produced a notably cleaner dimensional structure, particularly for Dimensions 3-5 which now tell a more interpretable story of variation among specific minority race/ethnicity groups.

  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(id = seq(n())) %>%
  select(id, `Dim 1`, `Dim 2`, `Dim 3`, `Dim 4`, `Dim 5`) %>%
  mutate(`Dim 1` = `Dim 1` / 100,
         `Dim 2` = `Dim 2` / 100,
         `Dim 3` = `Dim 3` / 100,
         `Dim 4` = `Dim 4` / 100,
         `Dim 5` = `Dim 5` / 100)

datatable(table) %>%
  formatPercentage(2:6, digits = 1)








Summary - Demographic Variables
Multiple Correspondence Analysis on the demographic variables produced five retained dimensions explaining 74.6% of the total variance. Dimension 1 captured an English language learner / Hispanic axis, driven by non.english.home, english.learner, and Hispanic ethnicity. Dimension 2 captured a special education / gender axis, Dimension 3 an American Indian / gender axis, and Dimensions 4 and 5 captured variation among minority race/ethnicity groups.
Overall, the MCA revealed that most demographic variables are capturing distinct and meaningful axes of variation, with the exception of some expected overlap between the language variables and Hispanic ethnicity. Given that this overlap is conceptually expected in a Southwest Minnesota context and that each variable retains some independent information, no demographic variables were eliminated following MCA.

COS2 - Postsecondary Variables
Overview COS2 measures the quality of representation of each variable category across the three retained dimensions. Values range considerably from 0.010 to 1.000, revealing both strong redundancy among some variables and poor representation of others.
Perfectly or Near-Perfectly Represented Categories Several categories achieve near-perfect total COS2 values, including ps.grad Attending ps (0.998), ps.grad.InstitutionSector Attending ps (0.998), highest.cred.level Attending ps (0.998), and ps.grad.location Attending ps (0.998). Similarly, ps.grad No (0.970), highest.cred.level Did not graduate ps (0.970), and ps.grad.location Did not graduate ps (0.972) are nearly identical in their representation. These patterns strongly suggest that these categories are capturing the same underlying variation across multiple variables, indicating considerable redundancy among ps.grad, ps.grad.location, and highest.cred.level.
Well Represented Categories ps.grad.InstitutionSector_4 (Public 2-year, 0.909), highest.cred.level Bachelor degree (0.767), and ps.grad.InstitutionSector Never attended ps (0.587) are well represented across the three retained dimensions.
Moderately Represented Categories attended.ps (0.587), ps.grad.InstitutionSector_1 (Public 4-year, 0.562), highest.cred.level Associate degree (0.451), and ps.grad.location PS grad outside MN (0.289) show moderate representation, suggesting some variation in these categories extends beyond the three retained dimensions.
Poorly Represented Categories Several categories show notably poor representation, including ps.grad.InstitutionSector_11 (Private other, 0.010), ps.grad.InstitutionSector_10 (Foreign institutions, 0.078), highest.cred.level Master degree or higher (0.099), and ps.grad.location PS grad region categories (0.170-0.188). These categories carry unique variation not well captured by the three retained dimensions.
Notes The near-identical COS2 patterns across ps.grad, ps.grad.location, and highest.cred.level for the Attending ps and Did not graduate ps categories strongly suggest redundancy among these variables that warrants careful consideration in variable retention decisions.

  as.data.frame() %>%
  select(`Dim 1`, `Dim 2`, `Dim 3`) %>%
  mutate(total = `Dim 1` + `Dim 2` + `Dim 3`)
  
datatable(table) %>%
  formatCurrency(1:4, "", digits = 3)




fviz_cos2(ps.mca, choice = "var", axes = 1:3)











MCA Contributions - Postsecondary Variables
Overview Contributions measure how much each variable category drives each retained dimension. Categories with higher contributions are the primary drivers of that dimension’s axis of variation. The contribution results reveal striking redundancy among several postsecondary variables, with near-identical contributions appearing across multiple variables for the same underlying construct.
Dimension 1 - Did Not Graduate Postsecondary Axis Dimension 1 is driven by near-identical contributions from attended.ps No (9.5%), ps.grad No (11.5%), highest.cred.level Did not graduate ps (11.5%), and ps.grad.location Did not graduate ps (11.5%). The near-identical contributions of these categories across four separate variables strongly indicates that these variables are capturing the same underlying construct — whether an individual did not attend or graduate from postsecondary education.
Dimension 2 - Currently Attending Postsecondary Axis Dimension 2 is almost entirely driven by four identical contributions of 21.8% each from ps.grad Attending ps, ps.grad.InstitutionSector Attending ps, highest.cred.level Attending ps, and ps.grad.location Attending ps. This perfect replication of contributions across four variables is unambiguous evidence of redundancy, as all four variables are capturing exactly the same information about individuals currently attending postsecondary education.
Dimension 3 - Institution Type and Credential Level Axis Dimension 3 is driven by ps.grad.InstitutionSector_4 (Public 2-year, 27.3%), highest.cred.level Bachelor degree (15.2%), highest.cred.level Less than Associate Degree (12.1%), and highest.cred.level Associate degree (13.7%). This dimension captures meaningful variation in the type of institution attended and the level of credential attained, representing the most substantively informative axis of variation among the postsecondary variables.
Notes The contribution results provide compelling evidence of redundancy among ps.grad, ps.grad.location, highest.cred.level, and attended.ps, particularly for the Attending ps and Did not graduate ps categories which contribute identically across multiple variables. This redundancy warrants serious consideration of variable elimination prior to modeling, with Dimension 3 suggesting that institution type and credential level may be the most informative non-redundant postsecondary variables.


table <- ps.mca$var$contrib %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  select(`Dim 1`, `Dim 2`, `Dim 3`) %>%
  mutate(`Dim 1` = `Dim 1` / 100,
         `Dim 2` = `Dim 2` /100,
         `Dim 3` = `Dim 3` / 100)

datatable(table) %>%
  formatPercentage(1:3, digits = 1)








MCA Summary - Postsecondary Variables
Multiple Correspondence Analysis on the postsecondary variables produced three retained dimensions explaining 52.9% of the total variance. Dimension 1 captured a did not graduate postsecondary axis, driven by near-identical contributions from attended.ps, ps.grad, highest.cred.level, and ps.grad.location, all reflecting whether an individual did not attend or complete postsecondary education. Dimension 2 captured a currently attending postsecondary axis, again driven by perfectly identical contributions across ps.grad, ps.grad.InstitutionSector, highest.cred.level, and ps.grad.location, providing unambiguous evidence of redundancy among these variables for this particular category. Dimension 3 captured a more substantively distinct axis of institution type and credential level, primarily driven by public 2-year institution attendance and varying credential levels.
While the MCA revealed considerable redundancy among the postsecondary variables, all five variables were retained on substantive grounds. Each variable contributes meaningful and distinct information to the modeling context, particularly given the importance of credential level distinctions, geographic location of attendance, and institution type in understanding regional workforce participation outcomes.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
section: Step 1: Data Preparation and Analytic Population
text:
Step 1: Data Preparation and Analytic Population
1.1 Analytic Population
The analytic population is restricted to individuals who:

Graduated from a high school in Southwest Minnesota, and
Did not complete a postsecondary credential (ps.grad = No), and
Have complete workforce participation categorizations for years 1 through 5 after high school or,
first 5 years after exiting attendance in a post-secondary institution.

1.2 Annual Workforce Participation Classification
For each individual, annual workforce participation status is identified for: - grad.year.1 - grad.year.2 - grad.year.3 - grad.year.4 - grad.year.5
Each year is classified into one of the following categories:

Meaningful workforce participation
Not meaningful workforce participation
No Minnesota employment record.

It should be noted that “grad.year.x” here means years after exiting formal education, not years after graduating high school.
1.3 Workforce Disconnection Indicators
For each annual observation, a binary disconnection indicator is created:

Disconnected (year-level) = Non-sustained WF - SW or MN, or No Minnesota emp record

Using these annual indicators, individuals are grouped based on persistence of disconnection across years 1–5:

Persistently Disconnected: Disconnected in 4 or 5 of the first 5 years
Disconnected (Broad): Disconnected in 3 of 5 years
Intermittently Disconnected: Disconnected in 1–2 of the first 5 years
Consistently Attached: Disconnected in 0 of the first 5 years

These categories emphasize sustained labor market attachment or detachment rather than point-in-time outcomes.
1.4 Regional Location of Not Meaningful Employment
For years in which individuals are categorized as Non-sustained WF, employment location is further classified as:

Within Southwest Minnesota
Outside Southwest Minnesota (elsewhere in Minnesota)
Both (simultaneous employment inside and outside the region)

This classification allows identification of regional underemployment versus regional disengagement.
1.5 Employment Intensity and Job Holding
For each individual and each year (years 1–5), the following employment intensity measures are constructed:

Number of distinct employers during the year
Indicator for multiple job holding (two or more employers)

These measures are used to distinguish underemployment from precarious or fragmented employment.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Step 2: Descriptive and Summary Statistics
2.1 Distribution of Workforce Disconnection
Summary statistics are produced to describe:

The proportion of non-college graduates in each workforce disconnection category
Differences in persistence and intermittency of disconnection

This establishes the overall scope and severity of workforce disconnection in early adulthood.
2.2 Regional Attachment and Job Structure
Among individuals experiencing workforce disconnection, summary statistics examine:

The location of not meaningful employment (within region, outside region, both)
Average and median number of employers per year
Prevalence of multiple job holding

These summaries clarify whether disconnection reflects local underemployment, out-of-region work, or fragmented employment patterns.

text:
Step 3: Relationship Between Individual Characteristics and Disconnection Trajectories
Step 3 will focus on answering the question of which characteristics are associated with the disconnection persistence categories. This will be a bi-variate analysis.
Independent Variables

3.2 Analytic Approach

Categorical variables are examined using cross-tabulations and measures of association (e.g., Cramer’s V).
Continuous variables are examined using ANOVA.
Interpretation emphasizes substantive differences and patterns rather than statistical significance alone.

3.3 Stratified and Comparative Analyses
Where sample sizes permit, additional analyses compare:

Persistently disconnected versus intermittently disconnected individuals
Individuals disconnected within the region versus outside the region
Individuals who transition into meaningful workforce participation versus those who do not

These comparisons help identify which characteristics are associated with stability, recovery, and regional retention.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Framing and Interpretation
This methodology prioritizes a trajectory-based understanding of workforce participation, recognizing that early-career labor market experiences are dynamic rather than static. By combining persistence measures, regional employment location, and job-holding intensity, the analysis aims to provide actionable insights for workforce development and labor force planning in Southwest Minnesota.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
section: Step 2: Identify Workforce State for 5 Years After Formal Education
text:
Step 2: Identify Workforce State for 5 Years After Formal Education
Next, we need to pull out all the individuals in which we have five years of workforce categories after they either graduate from high school or the last year in which they exited post-secondary attendance.
After that, we will categorize their workforce participation state into the following;

Sustained WF - SW
Sustained WF - MN
Non-sustained WF
No MN emp record.

I already created the annual workforce participation states for every individuals one year after graduation through 15 years after graduation. I will bring that list in and filter it by our analytic population.

annual.wf.states <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/States/annual-seven-states.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.year, states) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = fct_relevel(grad.year, "grad.year.0", "grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5", "grad.year.6", "grad.year.7", "grad.year.8", "grad.year.9", "grad.year.10", "grad.year.11", "grad.year.12", "grad.year.13", "grad.year.14", "grad.year.15")) 

no_ps_attendance <- analytic.pop %>%
  filter(attended.ps == "No") %>%
  select(PersonID) %>%
  left_join(annual.wf.states, by = "PersonID") %>%
  filter(states != "After 2023",
         states != "Attending ps",
         grad.year %in% c("grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5")) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(n == 5) %>%
  mutate(states = as_factor(states))

last_ps_attendance <- analytic.pop %>%
  filter(attended.ps == "Yes") %>%
  select(PersonID) %>%
  left_join(annual.wf.states, by = "PersonID") %>%
  filter(states != "After 2023") %>%
  mutate(numeric.grad.year = str_sub(grad.year, -2, -1),
         numeric.grad.year = str_replace(numeric.grad.year, "\\.", ""),
         numeric.grad.year = as.integer(numeric.grad.year)) %>%
  filter(states == "Attending ps") %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarize(last_ps_year = max(numeric.grad.year, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() 

ps_attendance <- annual.wf.states %>%
  right_join(last_ps_attendance, by = "PersonID") %>%
  filter(states != "After 2023") %>%
  mutate(numeric.grad.year = str_sub(grad.year, -2, -1),
         numeric.grad.year = str_replace(numeric.grad.year, "\\.", ""),
         numeric.grad.year = as.integer(numeric.grad.year),
         final.year = last_ps_year + 5) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  filter(numeric.grad.year <= final.year,
         numeric.grad.year > last_ps_year) %>%
  mutate(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(n == 5) %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.year, states, n) 

master.annual.wf.five.year.states <- ps_attendance %>%
  rbind(no_ps_attendance) %>%
  mutate(states = str_replace(states, "Not meaningful, not attending ps", "Non-sustained WF"),
         states = str_replace(states, "No MN emp record, not attending ps", "No MN emp record"),
         states = ifelse(states %in% c("Meaningful emp County", "Meaningful emp EDR", "Meaningful emp region"), "Sustained WF - SW", states),
         states = str_replace(states, "Meaningful emp MN", "Sustained WF - MN"),
         states = fct_relevel(states, "Sustained WF - SW", "Sustained WF - MN", "Non-sustained WF", "No MN emp record")) %>%
  select(-n) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  arrange(grad.year) %>%
  mutate(year.after.exit = seq(n())) %>%
  ungroup()

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Step 3: Workforce Disconnection Indicators
Next we add another category to determine the level of disconnection, if any, for each individual. Disconnected is defined as any individual that was categorized as not having meaningful workforce participation or no Minnesota employment record in a given year one through five years after exiting formal education.
The level of disconnection is defined as the following;

Persistently Disconnected: Disconnected in 4 or 5 of the first 5 years
Broadly Disconnected: Disconnected in 3 of the first 5 years
Intermittently Disconnected: Disconnected in 1–2 of the first 5 years
Consistently Attached: Disconnected in 0 of the first 5 years


disconnected.level <- master.annual.wf.five.year.states %>%
  mutate(disconnected = ifelse(states %in% c("Non-sustained WF", "No MN emp record"), "Disconnected", "Attached"),
         disconnected = as.factor(disconnected)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, disconnected) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  complete(PersonID, disconnected, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%
  filter(disconnected == "Disconnected") %>%
  mutate(disconnected.cat = ifelse(n == 0, "Consistently attached",
                                   ifelse(n %in% c(1,2), "Intermittently disconnected",
                                          ifelse(n == 3, "Broadly disconnected",
                                                 ifelse(n %in% c(4,5), "Persistently disconnected", "A")))),
         disconnected.cat = fct_relevel(disconnected.cat, "Consistently attached", "Intermittently disconnected", "Broadly disconnected", "Persistently disconnected"))

section: Step 4 & 5: Regional Location of Not Meaningful Employment
text:
Step 4 & 5: Regional Location of Not Meaningful Employment
For years in which individuals are categorized as not meaningfully attached to the workforce, employment location is further classified as: - Within Southwest Minnesota - Outside Southwest Minnesota (elsewhere in Minnesota) - Both (simultaneous employment inside and outside the region)
This classification allows identification of regional underemployment versus regional disengagement.
The population of individuals we need are the following;

Did not graduate college
For each individual categorize whether they had not meaningful workforce participation in the region, not in the region, or both.

We will use the master.annual.wf.five.year.states dataset as the starting point. We will have to have the year they graduated high school so when I match up employment records I’m only using employment records for the first 5 years after exiting formal education.

hs.grad.year <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/K12 Enrollment/K12Enrollment-master.csv")

         hs.grad.year = grad.year.y) %>%
  mutate(numeric.after.ed.year = str_sub(after.ed.year, -2, -1),
         numeric.after.ed.year = str_replace(numeric.after.ed.year, "\\.", ""),
         numeric.after.ed.year = as.integer(numeric.after.ed.year),
         emp.year = hs.grad.year + numeric.after.ed.year)

Now we need to bring in the employment data for Southwest graduates and then filter for PersonID that are in the newly created dataset. The columns we are going to keep from the employment dataset are the following;

PersonID: Identifies the graduate from Southwest Minnesota
TimeID: Last day of fiscal quarter
EmploymentOrganizationID: An internal identification for each employer.
EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked: The total number of hours worked by an employee at an employer’s location during a specific calendar quarter
EmployeeQuarterlyWages: The total wages earned by an employee at an employer’s location during a specific calendar quarter
EmployeeTenure: The total number of quarters a worker has been employeed by an organization at a specific location, up to an including the current calendar quarter
CountyName: The name of the county corresponding to the County and MNCounty Codes for this Location.


employment.original <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Employment/Employment-Southwest.csv") %>%
  drop_na(PersonID)

emp.year <- employment.original %>%
  filter(!is.na(TimeID)) %>%
  mutate(emp.year = str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4),
         emp.year = as.integer(emp.year),
         quarter = str_sub(TimeID, 5,6),
         quarter = ifelse(quarter == "03", 1,
                          ifelse(quarter == "06", 2,
                                 ifelse(quarter == "09", 3,
                                        ifelse(quarter == "12", 4, 0))))) %>%
  select(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked, EmployeeTenure, CountyName, emp.year, quarter) %>%
  mutate(CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Shakopee Mdewakanton Community", "Scott"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen")) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions.1[,c(1,2,10)], by = c("CountyName" = "Name"))

not.meaningful.pop.emp.year <- analytic.pop.annual.wf.states.hs.grad.year %>%
  filter(states == "Non-sustained WF") %>%
  select(PersonID, emp.year)

not.meaningful.emp.quarter <- not.meaningful.pop.emp.year %>%
  left_join(emp.year, by = c("PersonID", "emp.year")) %>%
  mutate(project.pr = ifelse(is.na(project.pr), "Unclassified", as.character(project.pr)),
         in_region = (project.pr == "Southwest"),
         unclassified_region = (project.pr == "Unclassified"),
         out_region = c(!in_region & !unclassified_region)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, emp.year, quarter) %>%
  summarise(n.emp = n(),
         any_in_quarter = any(in_region, na.rm = TRUE),
         any_out_quarter = any(out_region, na.rm = TRUE),
         any_unclassified_quarter = any(unclassified_region, na.rm = TRUE),
         any_mixed_qtr =  (sum(c(any_in_quarter, any_out_quarter, any_unclassified_quarter), na.rm = TRUE) >= 2)) %>%
  ungroup()

not.meaningful.emp.annual <- not.meaningful.emp.quarter %>%
  group_by(PersonID, emp.year) %>%
  summarize(multiple_emp_same_quarter = any(n.emp > 1),
            max_emp_in_qtr = max(n.emp),
            any_in_region = any(any_in_quarter, na.rm = TRUE),
            any_out_region = any(any_out_quarter, na.rm = TRUE),
            any_unclassified_region = any(any_unclassified_quarter, na.rm = TRUE),
            any_mixed_region = any(any_mixed_qtr, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(region_location_year = case_when(any_in_region & !any_out_region & !any_unclassified_region ~ "in_only", !any_in_region & any_out_region & !any_unclassified_region ~ "out_only", !any_in_region & !any_out_region & any_unclassified_region  ~ "unclassified_only", TRUE ~ "mixed" )) %>%
  mutate(
    mixed_type = case_when(
      region_location_year != "mixed" ~ NA_character_,
      any_in_region & any_out_region & !any_unclassified_region ~ "in_out",
      any_in_region & any_unclassified_region & !any_out_region ~ "in_unclassified",
      any_out_region & any_unclassified_region & !any_in_region ~ "out_unclassified",
      any_in_region & any_out_region & any_unclassified_region  ~ "in_out_unclassified"
    ),
    both_structure = case_when(region_location_year != "mixed" ~ NA_character_,
                               any_mixed_region ~ "simultaneous",
                               !any_mixed_region ~ "sequential",
                               TRUE ~ NA_character_)) %>%
  select(-any_in_region, -any_out_region, -any_unclassified_region, - any_mixed_region)

Next, we will piece this back together with the entire analytic population and create a complete annual workforce state for all individuals that did not complete post-secondary and has 5 years of workforce categories after graduating high school.

Master.not.meaningful <- not.meaningful.emp.annual %>%
  left_join(hs.grad.year[,c(1, 9)], by = "PersonID") %>%
  rename(hs.grad.year = grad.year) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = emp.year - hs.grad.year,
         grad.year = paste("grad.year.", grad.year, sep = "")) %>%
  complete(PersonID, grad.year) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = fct_relevel(grad.year, "grad.year.0", "grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5", "grad.year.6", "grad.year.7", "grad.year.8", "grad.year.9", "grad.year.10", "grad.year.11", "grad.year.12", "grad.year.13", "grad.year.14", "grad.year.15"))


Master.annual.wf.states.disconnected <- master.annual.wf.five.year.states %>%
  left_join(Master.not.meaningful, by = c("PersonID", "grad.year")) %>%
  unite("wf.states.refined",
        states, region_location_year, mixed_type, both_structure,
        sep = "_",
        na.rm = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(year.after.exit = paste("after.ed.", year.after.exit, sep = "")) %>%
  select(PersonID, year.after.exit, wf.states.refined) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year.after.exit, values_from = wf.states.refined) %>%
  left_join(disconnected.level[,c(1,4)], by = "PersonID")

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
section: Summary: What the Disconnection Analysis Tells Us
text:
Summary: What the Disconnection Analysis Tells Us
Persistent disconnection is the modal experience for non-college graduates in Southwest Minnesota, not a tail case. Of 13,177 non-college graduates with complete year 1–5 workforce records, half (50.4%) are persistently disconnected — disconnected (non-sustained participation or no MN employment record) in at least four of their first five years. Adding the broadly disconnected group (11.3%, disconnected in exactly 3 of 5 years) brings the total to roughly 62% spending the majority of their first five years disconnected. Only 14.0% are consistently attached in all five years — the smallest of the four persistence categories, outnumbered by the persistently disconnected group at roughly 3.6 to 1.
The annual trajectory shows the population diverging into two groups over time, not converging toward stability. Combined sustained participation (region + rest of MN) does rise steadily, from 32.1% in Year 1 to 42.0% by Year 5 — a real, incremental gain. But “no MN employment record” grows just as steadily over the same period, from 28.8% to 34.9%, and is the single largest category in every one of the five years. Meanwhile, non-sustained participation — in every subtype (in-region only, out-region only, mixed) — declines steadily across the five years. The net effect: people are moving out of non-sustained work, but into two different destinations. Some consolidate into sustained employment; a growing share drifts into having no detectable Minnesota employment record at all. By Year 5, having no MN record (34.9%) is a larger share of the population than either form of sustained employment individually.
The decline in non-sustained work is concentrated specifically in regional employment, not out-of-region employment. In-region-only non-sustained work nearly halves (19.7% → 10.8%), and mixed non-sustained work more than halves (11.2% → 5.0%), while out-region-only non-sustained work barely moves (7.8% → 7.0%). Whatever is driving people out of non-sustained status over the first five years, it’s happening disproportionately to those whose non-sustained work was in-region — they are either stabilizing into sustained work or dropping into no-record status, while out-of-region non-sustained workers are comparatively static year over year.
The more granular breakdown of “mixed” employment (simultaneous vs. sequential, and by location-tag combination) confirms rather than complicates this picture. Its decline tracks the aggregate mixed-category decline proportionally across all subtypes — no single subtype is driving the trend. The one substantive detail worth retaining: when non-sustained work spans both in- and out-of-region locations, it’s roughly 55–60% more often simultaneous (concurrent jobs in both places) than sequential (moving between locations within the year) in every year examined. The various “unclassified” location-tag combinations are consistently negligible (under ~1.6% combined in any year) and add no distinguishing signal.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
section: What this means going into the bivariate work
text:
What this means going into the bivariate work
Together, these tables reframe the disconnection story in two ways worth carrying into Step 3:

“No MN employment record” — not non-sustained employment — is the dominant and growing driver of disconnection. It’s already the largest single category by Year 1 and grows every year thereafter, while every non-sustained subtype shrinks. Since disconnection was defined as the union of these two states, most of the persistence finding (50.4% persistently disconnected) is likely attributable more to sustained absence from MN’s employment data than to cycling through unstable jobs. This distinction matters for framing: “persistently disconnected” sounds like a story about job instability, but the underlying pattern looks more like a story about growing disengagement from the Minnesota labor market entirely, whether that means informal work, out-of-state migration, unemployment, or something else not captured by wage records.
Given that persistent disconnection is the modal outcome (50.4%) and consistent attachment is the minority outcome (14.0%), the bivariate comparisons in Step 3 may be more informative anchored on persistently disconnected vs. everyone else, or on the four-category ordinal structure directly, rather than treating “consistently attached” as the default reference group — a 14%-sized reference group risks being an unrepresentative baseline for characterizing what predicts disconnection in this population.

  mutate(non_sustained.cat = ifelse(n == 0, "Never non-sustained",
                                    ifelse(n %in% c(1,2), "Intermittently non-sustained",

The majority of this population (74.4% combined: “never” + “intermittently” non-sustained) is not chronically cycling through unstable jobs — most non-sustained spells are short (intermittent, 1–2 years) or don’t happen at all. The earlier finding that 50.4% are “persistently disconnected” overall looks like it’s driven substantially more by sustained absence from MN wage records than by sustained job instability.

This reframes the modal story: rather than “most people are persistently stuck,” it reads as “most people have at least one rocky year, but relatively few are stuck in unstable work long-term.”
